113339.e: From about 1880, people began measuring the length of many Swiss glaciers every year. This series of measurements is one of the longest in the world.
113339.m: Switzerland has been measuring its glaciers for well over a hundred years.

113340.q: Which university leads GLAMOS together with universities such as Fribourg and Zurich?
a: University of Applied Sciences of the Grisons
113340.e: GLAMOS is run by ETH Zurich together with the universities of Fribourg and Zurich. Federal offices such as FOEN and MeteoSwiss support the network.
113340.m: ETH Zurich helps to lead GLAMOS.

113341.q: How do experts work out in spring how much snow is lying on a glacier?
a: They dig snow pits and measure depth and density
They weigh the glacier on a scale
They estimate it from tourists' photos
113341.e: In snow pits, they measure the depth of the snow and weigh snow samples. From this they calculate the amount of water that was added in winter.
113341.m: Snow pits show how much winter snow lies on a glacier.

113342.q: What do you measure when you work out the change in length of a glacier?
a: How far the glacier tongue has moved forward or back
How high above sea level the glacier is
How long a hiking path is
113342.e: Every year, the distance from a fixed point to the end of the glacier is measured. This shows whether the tongue is advancing or retreating.
113342.m: Measuring the length shows whether a glacier tongue is advancing or retreating.

113343.q: Besides measurements on site, what does GLAMOS use to record whole glaciers?
a: Weather balloons with cameras for animals
113343.e: From aerial photos, accurate elevation models of the glacier surface are calculated. Comparing them over the years shows how much volume has been lost.
113343.m: Aerial photos help to measure the volume of whole glaciers.

113344.q: Where in Switzerland is permafrost mainly found?
a: High in the mountains, often above about 2500 metres
Under fields on the Central Plateau
On the shores of Lake Geneva
In the forests of the Jura
113344.e: In the Swiss Alps, permafrost is found mainly in high, shady places. On north-facing slopes it often starts lower than on south-facing slopes.
113344.m: In Switzerland, permafrost is found mainly high in the mountains.

113345.q: What danger arises when permafrost thaws in steep rock faces?
113345.e: Frozen water in cracks in the rock acts like glue. When it thaws, the rock loses its hold, and stones or whole sections of rock can break off.
113345.m: Thawing permafrost makes rock faces unstable.

113346.q: What is measured in the Alps to keep an eye on permafrost?
113346.e: The Swiss monitoring network PERMOS measures the temperature in the ground in many places, as well as the movement of rock glaciers.
113346.m: Ground temperatures show how the permafrost is doing.

113347.q: What is a tongue-shaped mass of rock rubble and ice called that slowly creeps downhill in permafrost?
113347.e: A rock glacier is made of rubble mixed with ice. It creeps downhill like a thick paste, a few decimetres to a few metres a year.
113347.m: A rock glacier is creeping rubble with ice inside.

113348.q: Why do cable car stations in permafrost need special foundations?
a: Because the ground can sink or move when it thaws
Because there are no stones there
Because the ground is too warm
Because concrete is banned in the mountains
113348.e: When frozen ground thaws, it loses its strength. Foundations therefore have to be adjustable or anchored deep in the rock.
113348.m: Buildings in permafrost must be secured against movements in the ground.

113349.q: In which region of the Earth is permafrost especially widespread?
113349.e: In Siberia, Alaska and northern Canada, the ground is permanently frozen over large areas. In places, the permafrost there goes hundreds of metres deep.
113349.m: In Siberia, much of the ground is permanently frozen.

113350.q: Which greenhouse gas can be released from thawing permafrost?
113350.e: Plant remains are stored in the frozen ground. When it thaws, microbes break them down and release methane and carbon dioxide, which adds to the warming.

113351.q: What happens at the glacier tongue in summer?
a: More ice melts than snow is added
113351.e: The tongue lies low down and is warm. That is why a lot of ice melts there in summer.
113351.m: Ice melts at the glacier tongue.

113352.q: What do you call the very front end of the glacier tongue?
113352.e: The end of the tongue is called the glacier snout. That is where people measure whether the glacier is retreating or advancing.
113352.m: The very front end of a glacier is called the glacier snout.

113353.q: What happens to the glacier tongue when a glacier loses more ice than it gains over many years?
113353.e: With a negative mass balance, the tongue melts faster than ice flows down from above. It gets thinner and its end moves up the valley.
113353.m: When ice is lost, the glacier tongue retreats.

113354.q: How has the Lower Grindelwald Glacier changed since about 1850?
a: It has grown into the village
It has moved to a different mountain
113354.e: Around 1850, the Lower Grindelwald Glacier reached close to the village. Today its end lies much higher up in the gorge.
113354.m: The Lower Grindelwald Glacier once reached almost to the village.

113355.q: Why do you see bare ice instead of snow on the glacier tongue in summer?
a: The winter snow there has melted away
113355.e: Lower down, the winter snow melts completely in summer. Underneath, the older blue or grey glacier ice appears.
113355.m: In summer, there is bare ice on the glacier tongue.

113356.q: What often forms in a hollow in front of a retreating glacier tongue?
113356.e: The glacier has scraped out a hollow, which is often closed off by a moraine. When the tongue melts back, the hollow fills with meltwater.
113356.m: New lakes often form in front of melting glacier tongues.

113357.q: What breaks off when a glacier tongue ends in a lake or in the sea?
113357.e: At the edge in the water, blocks of ice break off and float away. This process is called calving.

113358.q: What is the stream called that flows out of the glacier mouth?
113358.e: The meltwater collects under the ice and comes out as a glacial stream. It carries a lot of cold, cloudy water.
113358.m: A glacial stream starts at the glacier mouth.

113359.q: Why is the water of a glacial stream often milky and cloudy?
113359.e: The glacier grinds rock into very fine flour. This floats in the water and makes it milky; people call it glacier milk.
113359.m: Rock flour makes glacier water milky.

113360.q: Why is it dangerous to go into a glacier mouth?
a: Pieces of ice can suddenly fall down
113360.e: The ice vault is constantly melting and can collapse without warning. The water level can also rise suddenly.
113360.m: Glacier mouths are dangerous because the ice can collapse.

113361.q: At what time of day does a glacial stream usually carry the most water in summer?
a: In the afternoon or early evening
113361.e: During the day, sun and warmth melt a lot of ice. It takes a few hours for the water to flow through the glacier, so the flow is greatest in the afternoon.
113361.m: In summer, glacial streams carry the most water in the afternoon.

113362.q: Why does the shape of a glacier mouth change from year to year?
a: Because meltwater and warmth keep wearing away the ice
Because it freezes over every year
113362.e: The flowing water and the summer warmth melt the ice around the opening. At the same time the tongue retreats, so the mouth moves or collapses.

113363.q: Where are the channels through which meltwater flows to the glacier mouth?
a: In the air above the glacier
113363.e: Meltwater seeps down through crevasses and moulins. Under the ice it forms a network of channels that leads to the glacier mouth.
113363.m: Meltwater flows in channels under the ice to the glacier mouth.

113364.q: What is a vertical shaft in a glacier called, through which meltwater plunges into the depths?
113364.e: Surface water falls into a shaft and swirls down into the depths. In this way, the water reaches the bottom of the glacier.
113364.m: In a moulin, water plunges deep into the glacier.

113365.q: Why do many glacier lakes shine turquoise?
a: Fine rock flour scatters the sunlight
113365.e: Tiny rock particles from the glacier float in the water. They mainly scatter blue and green light back.
113365.m: Rock flour turns glacier lakes turquoise.

a: A lake held back by a glacier acting as a dam
A lake that freezes over in winter
A lake in an ice rink
113366.e: When a glacier blocks a side valley, water collects behind it. Because the dam is made of ice, it can suddenly give way.
113366.m: An ice-dammed lake is held back by a glacier.

113367.q: What danger can come from a glacier lake?
a: A sudden flood wave if the dam breaks
113367.e: If a dam of ice or moraine breaks, the lake can empty all at once. The flood wave carries rubble with it and can put villages in danger.
113367.m: A bursting glacier lake can set off a dangerous flood wave.

113368.q: What can suddenly happen to a lake on a glacier in summer?
a: It drains through channels in the ice
113368.e: A lake forms on the Plaine Morte Glacier every year. It often empties in summer through a channel in the ice, and the water flows towards Lenk.
113368.m: Lakes on glaciers can suddenly empty.

113369.q: Why was a long suspension bridge built at the new Trift Lake?
a: The old path across the glacier had disappeared
So that cows could cross the lake
113369.e: When the Trift Glacier retreated, a lake formed. The old route across the ice was gone, so the Trift Bridge was built.
113369.m: Trift Lake formed when the Trift Glacier retreated.

113370.q: What are lakes called that form behind a ridge of glacier rubble?
113370.e: An end moraine can act like a natural dam. Meltwater collects behind it to form a moraine-dammed lake.
113370.m: Moraine-dammed lakes are held back by glacier rubble.

113371.q: Why are many new lakes forming in the Alps today?
a: Because the sea level is rising in the mountains
113371.e: Glaciers have scraped basins into the rock. When the ice melts, these basins fill with water.
113371.m: Where glaciers disappear, new lakes often form.

113372.q: How did big lakes on the Swiss Central Plateau such as Lake Zurich form?
a: Ice Age glaciers scraped out their basins
113372.e: During the Ice Ages, huge glaciers flowed from the Alps into the Central Plateau. They gouged out deep basins, which later filled with water.
113372.m: Many Swiss lakes lie in basins scraped out by glaciers.

113373.q: Roughly how many years ago did the last Ice Age end?
113373.e: The last cold period ended about 11,700 years ago. Since then we have been living in a warm period, the Holocene.
113373.m: The last Ice Age ended almost 12,000 years ago.

113374.q: What is the last Ice Age in the Alps called, named after a river in Bavaria?
113374.e: The Alpine glaciations were named after rivers north of the Alps. The most recent is called the Würm glaciation, after the River Würm in Bavaria.
113374.m: The last Ice Age in the Alps is called the Würm glaciation.

113375.q: What are big boulders called that glaciers carried far from where they came from during the Ice Age?
113375.e: Glaciers carried boulders from the Alps as far as the Central Plateau and the Jura. They lie there today as erratics, often made of rock that is not otherwise found there.
113375.m: Erratic boulders were carried far by glaciers.

113376.q: Which large animal also lived in the area of present-day Switzerland during the last Ice Age?
113376.e: The woolly mammoth was adapted to the cold with its thick coat. Bones and tusks have been found in Switzerland, for example near Niederweningen.
113376.m: Mammoths lived in Switzerland too during the Ice Age.

113377.q: How did the sea level during the last Ice Age compare with today?
113377.e: Huge amounts of water were locked up in ice sheets on the continents. That is why the sea level was about 120 metres lower than today.
113377.m: During the Ice Age, the sea level was much lower than today.

113378.q: Which land bridge was dry during the last Ice Age and connected Asia with North America?
113378.e: Because the sea level was low, the Bering Strait was dry land. People and animals reached America across this land bridge.
113378.m: During the Ice Age, people reached America via Beringia.

113379.q: What did much of the Swiss Central Plateau look like during the last Ice Age?
a: It was covered by glacier ice
It was flooded by a sea
113379.e: At their greatest extent, about 20,000 years ago, large Alpine glaciers flowed far into the Central Plateau. Large parts of it lay under ice.
113379.m: During the Ice Age, much of the Central Plateau lay under ice.

113380.q: Which glacier carried rock from Valais as far as the area around Solothurn during the last Ice Age?
113380.e: The Ice Age Rhône Glacier flowed from Valais through the Lake Geneva basin into the Central Plateau. It reached as far as the area around Solothurn and Wangen an der Aare.
113380.m: The Ice Age Rhône Glacier reached the Central Plateau near Solothurn.

113381.q: What kind of period are we living in today, now that the last Ice Age is over?
113381.e: During the Ice Age era, long cold periods alternated with shorter warm periods. For about 11,700 years we have been living in a warm period, which experts also call an interglacial.
113381.m: Between two Ice Ages there is a warm period.

113382.q: Why must you never use a plugged-in hairdryer near a full bath?
a: Because bath water conducts electricity and there is a risk of electric shock
Because the hairdryer would get too loud
Because the water would boil immediately
Because the hairdryer would then use less electricity
113382.e: Tap water contains dissolved substances and conducts electricity. If the hairdryer falls into the water, current can flow through the body, which can kill.
113382.m: Electrical appliances must be kept away from bath water.

113383.q: What happens to a lamp in a circuit when you open the switch?
113383.e: An open switch breaks the circuit. Without a closed path no current can flow, and the lamp goes out.
113383.m: An open switch breaks the circuit.

113384.e: Salt water contains dissolved salt particles that can carry electric charge. Pure, distilled water, on the other hand, conducts very poorly.
113384.m: Dissolved salt makes water a good conductor.

113385.q: Why is a cable covered in plastic on the outside?
a: To protect against electric shocks and short circuits
So that the current flows faster
So that the cable produces more voltage
113385.e: Plastic conducts practically no electricity. The covering protects people from touching the wire and stops bare conductors touching each other.
113385.m: The plastic covering of a cable protects against electric shocks.

113386.q: Why can a cable get very hot in a short circuit?
a: Because a very large current flows
Because no current flows at all
113386.e: In a short circuit the device with its resistance is missing. So a very large current flows, which heats the wire strongly.
113386.m: A short circuit produces a dangerously large current.

113387.q: What is a device in a circuit called that turns electrical energy into another form of energy, for example a lamp?
113387.e: Lamps, motors or heaters are called loads. They turn electrical energy into light, movement or heat.

113388.q: Which component supplies the electrical energy in a simple circuit?
113388.e: The battery is the voltage source. It drives the current and supplies the energy that the lamp turns into light.
113388.m: The battery is the source in the circuit.

113389.q: What is the direction of the so-called conventional current outside the source?
a: From the positive terminal to the negative terminal
From the negative terminal to the positive terminal
Always in a circle around the source
From the device back to the socket
113389.e: It was agreed long ago that current flows from plus to minus. In reality the electrons move the other way, but the rule is still used.
113389.m: Conventional current points from plus to minus.

113390.q: Why does a lamp not light up if you connect both wires only to the positive terminal of a battery?
a: The circuit is not closed across both terminals
113390.e: Current only flows if there is a path from one terminal to the other. Between two connections on the same terminal there is no voltage.
113390.m: A lamp needs a connection to both terminals of the source.

113391.q: How are two lamps connected in a series circuit?
a: One after the other on a single current path
With no connection to the source
113391.e: In a series circuit the current flows through all the devices one after the other. There is no branching.
113391.m: In a series circuit all devices are on one single path.

113392.q: How is a light switch connected to the lamp it switches on and off?
113392.e: The switch must be able to break the lamp's current path. So it is on the same path as the lamp, in other words in series.
113392.m: A switch is in series with the device it switches.

113393.q: How big is the current at different points in a series circuit?
113393.e: There is only one current path, and no charge is lost. So the same current flows through every component.
113393.m: In a series circuit the current is the same everywhere.

113394.q: Two identical lamps are connected in series to 12 V. What voltage is across each lamp?
113394.e: In a series circuit the total voltage is shared. With two identical lamps, each gets half: 12 V ÷ 2 = 6 V.
113394.m: In a series circuit the voltage is shared between the devices.

113395.q: In a series circuit there are 2 V, 3 V and 4 V across three components. What is the voltage of the source?
113395.e: In a series circuit the individual voltages add up to the total voltage: 2 V + 3 V + 4 V = 9 V.
113395.m: The individual voltages in a series circuit add up to the total voltage.

113396.q: How does the brightness change if you add a second identical lamp in series to a lamp?
a: Both shine more weakly than the one did before
Both shine as brightly as the one did before
113396.e: The total resistance gets bigger, and each lamp only gets half the voltage. So less current flows and both shine more weakly.
113396.m: More lamps in series shine more weakly.

113397.q: How do you connect three 1.5 V batteries to get a voltage of 4.5 V?
a: Only two of them in parallel
113397.e: When batteries are connected in series, their voltages add up: 1.5 V + 1.5 V + 1.5 V = 4.5 V.
113397.m: Batteries in series add their voltages.

113398.q: Two resistors of 10 ohms and 20 ohms are connected in series. What is the total resistance?
113398.e: In a series circuit the resistances add up: 10 ohms + 20 ohms = 30 ohms.

113399.q: What happens in a series circuit with two lamps if one lamp blows?
a: The other lamp shines more brightly
The other lamp keeps shining just as brightly
The battery goes flat at once
113399.e: In a series circuit there is only one current path. If one lamp is broken, no current can flow anywhere.
113399.m: In a series circuit one faulty device breaks the whole circuit.

113400.q: How are the lamps connected in a parallel circuit?
a: Each lamp on its own branch to the same source
All one after the other on one path
Only one lamp to the source
Without a switch and without a source
113400.e: In a parallel circuit the circuit branches. Each lamp is connected separately to both terminals of the source.
113400.m: In a parallel circuit each device has its own branch.

113401.q: What happens in a parallel circuit with two lamps if one lamp blows?
113401.e: Each branch is closed on its own. If one branch fails, current still flows in the other branch.
113401.m: In a parallel circuit the devices work independently of each other.

113402.q: How brightly do two identical lamps in parallel on a battery shine compared with a single lamp on the same battery?
113402.e: In a parallel circuit each lamp gets the full voltage of the battery. So the same current flows through each as through a single lamp.
113402.m: Lamps in parallel shine as brightly as when connected on their own.

113403.q: How are the sockets and lamps in a flat connected to the mains?
a: Alternately in series and in parallel
Not connected to each other at all
113403.e: Every device should get the full mains voltage and be able to be switched on and off by itself. That is only possible with a parallel circuit.
113403.m: Household devices are connected to the mains in parallel.

113404.q: In a parallel circuit, 0.2 A flows through one lamp and 0.3 A through the other. What is the total current?
113404.e: In a parallel circuit the branch currents add up to the total current: 0.2 A + 0.3 A = 0.5 A.
113404.m: In a parallel circuit the branch currents add up to the total current.

113405.q: 1.2 A flows through the main line of a parallel circuit. 0.5 A flows through one branch. What is the current in the second branch?
113405.e: The total current divides between the branches. That leaves 1.2 A minus 0.5 A, which is 0.7 A, for the second branch.
113405.m: In a parallel circuit the total current divides between the branches.

113406.q: What is the point called where a circuit splits into several branches?
113406.e: At a junction three or more wires meet. There the current divides or flows back together.
113406.m: At a junction the current branches.

113407.q: How does the total current from the battery change if you add another lamp in parallel?
113407.e: Each extra lamp opens another path for the current. The total current is the sum of all the branch currents and so gets bigger.
113407.m: Each new parallel branch increases the total current.

113408.q: Which device has a circle with a cross inside as its circuit symbol?
113408.e: In circuit diagrams a filament lamp is drawn as a circle with a diagonal cross. The cross is a reminder of the filament.
113408.m: A circle with a cross stands for a lamp.

113409.q: In the circuit symbol for a battery, what does the longer of the two lines mean?
113409.e: A battery cell is drawn with one long and one short line. The long line is the positive terminal, the short one the negative terminal.
113409.m: In the battery symbol the long line stands for plus.

113410.q: Which component is shown as a small rectangle according to the European standard?
113410.e: In Europe a resistor is drawn as a long rectangle. In American diagrams a zigzag line is drawn instead.
113410.m: A rectangle in a circuit diagram stands for a resistor.

113411.q: Which device has a circle with a large M inside as its circuit symbol?
113411.e: In circuit diagrams the letter M stands for motor. An electric motor turns electrical energy into movement.
113411.m: A circle with M stands for an electric motor.

113412.q: How is an open switch drawn in a circuit diagram?
a: As a line sticking out at an angle, with a gap
As a circle with a cross
113412.e: An open switch is drawn like a raised drawbridge. The gap shows that the circuit is broken.
113412.m: An open switch has a gap in its symbol.

113413.q: Which component is drawn as a triangle with a line across its tip and two small arrows pointing outwards?
113413.e: The triangle with a line is the symbol for a diode. The two arrows pointing outwards show that the diode gives off light, so it is an LED.
113413.m: An LED is drawn as a diode with light arrows.

113414.q: Why are circuit symbols used instead of pictures of the real components?
a: They are simple, clear and understood everywhere
Their colours are set by law
They show the exact size of the components
113414.e: Circuit symbols are standardised and reduced to the essentials. This lets experts all over the world read circuit diagrams quickly.
113414.m: Standard circuit symbols make diagrams clear.

113415.q: How is a point where two wires are connected shown in a circuit diagram?
113415.e: A thick dot at a crossing means the wires are connected. If lines cross without a dot, they are not connected.
113415.m: A dot in a circuit diagram shows that wires are connected.

a: A drawing of a circuit with standard symbols
A list of all the sockets in the house
113416.e: A circuit diagram uses symbols and lines to show how the components of a circuit are connected.
113416.m: A circuit diagram shows a circuit with symbols.

113417.q: How are the wires usually drawn in a circuit diagram?
a: As straight lines with right angles
113417.e: Wires are drawn horizontally and vertically wherever possible. This keeps the diagram clear, even if the real cables are not straight.
113417.m: In a circuit diagram wires are drawn straight and at right angles.

113418.q: What does a circuit diagram not show?
a: The exact position and length of the cables
Whether components are in series or in parallel
113418.e: A circuit diagram only shows the electrical connections. Where the cables actually run and how long they are cannot be seen from it.
113418.m: A circuit diagram shows connections, not the real position of the components.

113419.q: In a circuit diagram, a battery, a switch and two lamps are on a single closed line with no branches. Which circuit is this?
113419.e: Without branches, the current flows through all the components one after the other. That is the sign of a series circuit.
113419.m: A circuit without branches is a series circuit.

113420.q: How can you recognise a parallel circuit in a circuit diagram?
a: By the wire branching into several branches
113420.e: In a parallel circuit the wire splits into several paths at junctions. Each path has its own component.
113420.m: Branches in a circuit diagram show a parallel circuit.

113421.q: In a circuit diagram, a switch is in the main line before a branch to two lamps. What does it do?
a: It only switches the first lamp
It only switches the second lamp
113421.e: All the current flows through the main line. If you open the switch there, both branches are broken.
113421.m: A switch in the main line switches all the branches.

113422.q: What happens if you bridge a lamp in a circuit diagram directly with a wire?
a: The lamp is short-circuited and does not light
The lamp shines just as brightly
113422.e: The current takes the path with the least resistance through the bridge. Practically no current then flows through the lamp.

113423.q: Which circuit does a diagram show in which the stairwell light can be switched from two places?
113423.e: With two two-way switches you can switch a lamp on and off from two places. This circuit is called two-way switching and is common in stairwells.
113423.m: With two-way switching you switch a lamp from two places.

113424.q: What does electrical voltage tell you?
a: How strong the push driving the current is
How many cables are in the circuit
113424.e: Voltage is the push that moves the charges through the circuit. The bigger the voltage, the more strongly they are pushed.

113425.q: Which symbol is used for electrical voltage in German formulas?
113425.e: In German formulas U stands for voltage (in English, V is also common). Its unit is the volt.
113425.m: The formula symbol for voltage is U.

113426.q: In Switzerland, cookers are often connected to a high-power (three-phase) supply. What voltage does it have?
113426.e: Normal sockets have 230 V. Powerful appliances such as cookers use the three-phase supply with 400 V.
113426.m: The household three-phase supply has 400 volts.

113427.q: What does a battery supply: direct voltage or alternating voltage?
113427.e: With a battery, the positive and negative terminals always stay the same. So the current always flows in the same direction.

113428.q: What is the device called that turns the mains voltage into a small, adjustable voltage for experiments at school?
113428.e: A power supply unit is plugged into the socket and gives a safe low voltage. This can often be adjusted smoothly.
113428.m: A power supply unit gives small voltages for experiments.

113429.q: Why is mains voltage dangerous for people, but a 1.5 V battery is not?
a: The high voltage can drive a dangerously large current through the body
The body only conducts with batteries
113429.e: The bigger the voltage, the more current can flow through the body. At mains voltage the current can endanger the heart; at 1.5 V it is far too small.

113430.q: Where in a circuit is there a voltage even when the switch is open?
a: Between the terminals of the battery
113430.e: A battery always has a voltage across its terminals, even when no current flows. But current only flows once the circuit is closed.
113430.m: A voltage can be there even when no current flows.

113431.q: At what voltage do most SBB trains run via the overhead line?
113431.e: The SBB's overhead lines carry an alternating voltage of 15,000 volts, which is 15 kilovolts. The locomotive converts it for its motors.

113432.q: Which country did Alessandro Volta, after whom the unit volt is named, come from?
113432.e: Alessandro Volta was born in Como in 1745 and taught at the University of Pavia. He was one of the most important pioneers of electricity.
113432.m: Alessandro Volta was an Italian physicist.

113433.q: What is the first battery that Alessandro Volta built around 1800 called?
113433.e: Volta stacked metal discs and cardboard soaked in salt water on top of each other in turn. This pile was the first to supply a lasting electric current.
113433.m: The voltaic pile was the first battery.

113434.q: Which metals were the discs of a voltaic pile typically made of?
113434.e: Volta stacked discs of zinc and copper, sometimes silver, with damp cardboard in between. A voltage forms between the different metals.
113434.m: Two different metals in salt water produce a voltage.

113435.q: How many volts are there in 1 kilovolt?
113435.e: The prefix kilo means thousand. So 1 kV = 1000 V.
113435.m: One kilovolt is a thousand volts.

113436.m: One volt is a thousand millivolts.

113437.q: What voltage does the starter battery of an ordinary car have?
113437.e: Most cars have a 12-volt battery. It supplies the current for the starter motor and the on-board electronics.

113438.q: Roughly what voltage does a single lithium-ion cell, like the ones in mobile phones, have?
113438.e: A lithium-ion cell has a nominal voltage of about 3.6 to 3.7 volts. That is much more than an ordinary battery cell.
113438.m: A lithium-ion cell has around 3.7 volts.

113440.q: What does electric current tell you?
a: How much charge flows through a conductor per second
113440.e: Current tells you how much electric charge flows through a cross-section of the conductor every second.
113440.m: Current measures how much charge flows per second.

113441.q: Which formula symbol is used for current?
113441.e: Current has the formula symbol I. It comes from the French word “intensité”.
113441.m: The formula symbol for current is I.

113442.q: Which formula do you use to work out current from voltage and resistance?
113442.e: According to Ohm's law, U = R × I. Rearranging for I gives I = U / R.
113442.m: Current is voltage divided by resistance.

113443.q: How does the current change if, with the same voltage, you use a resistance twice as big?
113443.e: According to I = U / R, the current gets smaller when the resistance gets bigger. With double the resistance, only half as much current flows.
113443.m: Double the resistance means half the current at the same voltage.

113444.q: What happens to the current through a lamp if you increase the voltage?
113444.e: A bigger voltage pushes the current harder. So more current flows and the lamp shines more brightly.

113445.q: At what current is an ordinary small LED typically run?
113445.e: Small standard LEDs are usually designed for about 20 milliamps. A series resistor makes sure the current doesn't get too big.
113445.m: Small LEDs only need a few milliamps.

113446.q: Which effect of electric current does a kettle use?
113446.e: When current flows through the heating element, it gets hot. The heat is passed on to the water.
113446.m: A kettle uses the heating effect of current.

113447.q: Which effect of electric current is used to copper-plate or gold-plate objects?
113447.e: When current flows through a metal salt solution, metal is deposited on the object. This process is called electroplating.
113447.m: Electroplating uses the chemical effect of current.

113448.q: Which effect of electric current does an electromagnet use?
113448.e: Every conductor carrying a current produces a magnetic field. In a coil with an iron core it becomes so strong that it attracts iron.

113449.q: Who is the unit ampere named after?
113449.e: In the 19th century the physicist André-Marie Ampère studied the magnetic effect of current. In his honour the unit of current is called the ampere.
113449.m: The unit ampere honours André-Marie Ampère.

113450.q: Which country did André-Marie Ampère come from?
113450.e: Ampère was born in Lyon in 1775 and worked in Paris. He is seen as one of the founders of electrodynamics.
113450.m: André-Marie Ampère was a French physicist.

113451.q: How many milliamps are there in 1 amp?
113451.e: The prefix milli means one thousandth. So 1 A = 1000 mA.
113451.m: One amp is a thousand milliamps.

113452.m: Divide milliamps by a thousand to get amps.

113453.q: Which abbreviation stands for the unit ampere?
113453.e: The unit ampere is abbreviated with the capital letter A. Instruments for measuring current also carry this symbol.
113453.m: The abbreviation for ampere is A.

113454.q: What is true of the ampere in the International System of Units (SI)?
a: It is one of the seven base units
It is not an official unit
It is a unit of voltage
It is a unit of energy
113454.e: The SI has seven base units, including the metre, kilogram, second and ampere. The volt, on the other hand, is a derived unit.
113454.m: The ampere is an SI base unit.

113455.q: Roughly what current is typical in a lightning strike?
113455.e: In a lightning strike, typically tens of thousands of amps flow for a very short time. That is why lightning is so dangerous.
113455.m: Huge currents flow in a lightning strike.

113456.q: What current is already dangerous for a person if it flows through the body?
113456.e: Even currents of a few dozen milliamps can upset the rhythm of the heart. That is why safety switches in homes are set to be very sensitive.
113456.m: Even small currents through the body can kill.

113457.q: What is the minimum number of ammeters you need to measure both branch currents at the same time in a parallel circuit with two lamps?
113457.e: Each branch has its own current. To measure both at the same time, each branch needs its own ammeter.
113457.m: Each branch current needs its own ammeter.

113458.q: How is an ammeter placed in a circuit?
a: With no connection to the circuit
113458.e: All the current you want to measure must flow through the ammeter. So it is inserted into the circuit, in other words connected in series.
113458.m: An ammeter is connected in series.

113459.q: Why does an ammeter have a very small internal resistance?
a: So that it hardly changes the current in the circuit
So that it produces more voltage
113459.e: The ammeter sits in the current path. If it had a large resistance, it would slow the current and give a false reading.
113459.m: A good ammeter has a very small resistance.

113460.q: What can happen if you connect an ammeter directly to the terminals of a battery?
a: A short circuit that can damage the meter
113460.e: Because of its small resistance, a very large current then flows. The fuse in the meter can blow or the meter gets damaged.
113460.m: An ammeter must never be connected directly to the source.

113461.q: What does the circuit symbol for an ammeter look like?
a: A circle with an A inside
A circle with a V inside
A rectangle with an A inside
A triangle with an A inside
113461.e: Meters are drawn as circles. The letter A shows that amps, in other words current, are being measured.
113461.m: An ammeter is drawn as a circle with an A.

113462.q: An ammeter is set to the 1 A range. The pointer is exactly in the middle of the scale. What current is flowing?
113462.e: Full deflection at the end of the scale matches the 1 A range. The middle of the scale means half of that: 1 A ÷ 2 = 0.5 A.
113462.m: When reading a meter, always note the range it is set to.

113463.q: Where must you place the ammeter to measure the total current of a parallel circuit?
a: In the main line before the branch
113463.e: The current of all the branches flows together through the main line. So an ammeter there measures the total current.
113463.m: You measure the total current in the main line.

113464.q: What does an ammeter show when the switch in the circuit is open?
113464.e: With the switch open, the circuit is broken. No current flows, so the ammeter shows zero.
113464.m: Without a closed circuit the ammeter shows zero.

113465.e: A voltmeter shows what voltage there is between two points in a circuit. The reading is in volts.

113466.q: How is a voltmeter connected to measure the voltage across a lamp?
a: Only to one terminal of the lamp
In series between the lamp and the switch
113466.e: Voltage exists between two points. So you connect the voltmeter to both terminals of the lamp, in other words in parallel.
113466.m: A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component.

113467.q: Why does a voltmeter have a very large internal resistance?
a: So that hardly any current flows through the meter
So that it doubles the voltage
113467.e: The voltmeter sits in parallel with the component. Because of the large resistance almost no current flows through it, and the circuit is hardly affected.
113467.m: A good voltmeter has a very large resistance.

113468.q: What does the circuit symbol for a voltmeter look like?
a: A circle with a V inside
A circle with an A inside
A circle with a cross inside
A rectangle with a V inside
113468.e: Meters are drawn as circles. The V shows that voltage is measured in volts.
113468.m: A voltmeter is drawn as a circle with a V.

113469.q: A voltmeter is held against the terminals of a new flat 4.5 V battery. Roughly what reading does it show?
113469.e: A new flat battery has a nominal voltage of 4.5 V. The voltmeter shows roughly this value.

113470.q: What does a voltmeter show when connected across a closed switch in a circuit?
113470.e: A closed switch is a good conductor with almost no resistance. So practically no voltage is dropped across its terminals.
113470.m: There is almost no voltage across a closed switch.

113471.q: What does a voltmeter show across an open switch in a simple circuit with a battery and a lamp?
113471.e: With the switch open no current flows, and no voltage is dropped across the lamp. So the whole battery voltage is across the gap in the switch.
113471.m: The whole voltage of the source is across an open switch.

113472.q: What happens if you wrongly connect a voltmeter in series with the lamp?
a: The lamp hardly lights because almost no current flows
113472.e: The large internal resistance of the voltmeter lets almost no current through. The lamp stays dark, and the voltmeter shows roughly the battery voltage.
113472.m: A voltmeter in series blocks the current almost completely.

a: A meter for several electrical quantities
A device that only measures time
113473.e: Depending on the setting, a multimeter can measure voltage, current and resistance. That is why it has its name.
113473.m: A multimeter measures different electrical quantities.

113474.q: Which socket of a multimeter is the black test lead usually connected to?
113474.e: COM stands for “common”, the shared reference socket. The black lead stays there for almost all measurements; the red one is moved depending on the measurement.
113474.m: The black test lead goes in the COM socket.

113475.q: What does a multimeter measure on the setting A with a straight line next to it?
113475.e: The A stands for amps, in other words current. The straight line means direct current, like that from a battery.
113475.m: A with a straight line means direct current.

113476.q: Why do you only measure a resistance with a multimeter when the circuit is switched off?
a: Because the meter itself produces a small measuring current
Because resistances can only be measured at night
Because the resistance would otherwise disappear
Because the display would otherwise be too bright
113476.e: To measure resistance, the multimeter sends its own small current through the component. Other voltages would give a false reading or damage the meter.
113476.m: Resistances are only measured in circuits with no power.

113477.q: Which range do you choose on a multimeter if you don't know how big the voltage is?
113477.e: If you start with the largest range, the meter cannot be overloaded. Then you switch step by step to smaller ranges for more precise values.
113477.m: With unknown values, start with the largest range.

113478.q: What does a wavy line (~) next to the V on a multimeter show?
113478.e: The wavy line stands for alternating voltage, like that from a socket. Straight lines, on the other hand, mark direct voltage.
113478.m: A wavy line means alternating voltage.

113479.q: What does a minus sign in front of the reading mean when measuring direct voltage with a multimeter?
a: The test leads are connected the wrong way round
113479.e: The multimeter also shows the direction of the voltage. If you hold the red lead to minus and the black one to plus, a minus sign appears.
113479.m: A minus sign shows the test leads are swapped.

113480.q: What is the continuity test on a multimeter, where the meter beeps, used for?
a: To check whether a wire is connected all the way through
113480.e: In the continuity test, the meter beeps if there is a very small resistance between the probes. This lets you quickly find broken cables.
113480.m: With the continuity test you find broken wires.

113481.q: Which socket of a multimeter do you plug the red lead into to measure large currents of a few amps?
113481.e: For large currents a multimeter has its own specially protected socket, usually labelled 10A. The mA socket is only meant for small currents.
113481.m: Large currents are measured through the 10A socket.

113482.q: What is the continent around the South Pole called?
113482.e: Antarctica is the continent on which the South Pole lies. The Arctic, on the other hand, is the area around the North Pole and consists mainly of frozen sea.
113482.m: The continent of Antarctica lies at the South Pole.

113483.q: What lowest air temperature was measured at a research station in Antarctica in 1983?
113483.e: On 21 July 1983, -89.2 °C was measured at a Russian station in the interior of the continent. That is the lowest air temperature ever measured directly on Earth.
113483.m: The lowest air temperature on Earth was measured in Antarctica.

113484.q: Roughly what percentage of Antarctica's surface is covered by ice?
113484.e: Almost the whole continent lies under a thick layer of ice. Only about 2 per cent of the surface, mainly mountain tops and strips of coast, is free of ice.
113484.m: Antarctica is almost completely covered in ice.

113485.q: What is the highest mountain in Antarctica called?
113485.e: Mount Vinson in the Ellsworth Mountains is about 4900 metres high. That makes it a little higher than the Dufourspitze, the highest peak in Switzerland.
113485.m: Mount Vinson is the highest mountain in Antarctica.

113486.q: Why is Antarctica considered a desert despite all the ice?
a: Because very little rain or snow falls there
Because there is a lot of sand there
Because the sun never shines there
113486.e: A desert is defined by how little rain or snow falls, not by heat or sand. In the interior of Antarctica, very little snow falls each year.
113486.m: Antarctica is a cold desert because hardly any rain or snow falls there.

113487.q: Which ocean surrounds the continent of Antarctica?
113487.e: The Southern Ocean completely surrounds Antarctica. The Antarctic Circumpolar Current flows in it all the way around the continent.
113487.m: Antarctica is surrounded on all sides by the Southern Ocean.

113488.q: How many people live permanently in Antarctica?
a: None, only researchers for a while
113488.e: There is no permanent population in Antarctica. Researchers and station staff only stay for a few months; in summer there are several thousand people.
113488.m: Nobody lives in Antarctica permanently; only researchers work there for a while.

113489.q: Which mountain range divides Antarctica into East and West Antarctica?
113489.e: The Transantarctic Mountains stretch for about 3500 kilometres right across the continent. They separate the larger East Antarctica from the smaller West Antarctica.
113489.m: The Transantarctic Mountains separate East and West Antarctica.

113490.q: In which months is it summer in Antarctica?
113490.e: Antarctica is in the Southern Hemisphere, where the seasons are the other way round from Europe. That is why most expeditions take place during our winter.
113490.m: When it is winter here, it is summer in Antarctica.

113491.q: Who reached the South Pole before Robert Falcon Scott?
113491.e: The Norwegian Roald Amundsen stood at the South Pole on 14 December 1911. Scott arrived just over a month later.
113491.m: Amundsen reached the South Pole before Scott.

113492.q: How did the return journey of Scott's group from the South Pole end in 1912?
a: They all returned safe and well
113492.e: On the march back, the men suffered from cold, hunger and exhaustion. None of the five men who reached the pole came back alive.
113492.m: Scott's whole polar group died on the way back.

113493.q: Why did Scott's seriously ill companion Lawrence Oates walk out alone into the blizzard?
a: He did not want to hold up his companions
He wanted to take a shortcut to the ship
113493.e: Oates had badly frostbitten feet and could only move slowly. He went out so that the others could move on faster without him.
113493.m: Lawrence Oates sacrificed himself so as not to slow down his companions.

113494.q: Which animals did Scott take to pull sledges, which coped badly with the cold?
113494.e: Among other things, Scott relied on ponies from Manchuria. The animals sank into the snow, suffered from the cold and had to be killed.
113494.m: Scott's ponies were poorly suited to the ice of Antarctica.

113495.q: How do we know so much today about the last weeks of Scott's group?
a: From Scott's diary, which was found
From film footage of the journey
113495.e: In November 1912, search parties found the tent with the dead men and Scott's diary. His entries describe their hardship until the last days.
113495.m: Scott's diary tells of the tragic end of his expedition.

113496.q: Roughly how far was Scott's last camp from the next big supply depot?
113496.e: The tent was only about 11 miles, or about 18 kilometres, from the so-called One Ton Depot. A blizzard stopped the weakened men from going on.
113496.m: Scott's group died only about 18 kilometres from a supply depot.

113497.q: What did Scott and his men find at the South Pole in January 1912?
a: A tent with the flag of Norway
Nothing at all; they were the first
113497.e: Amundsen had arrived just over a month before Scott and had left a tent with a Norwegian flag. For Scott's group, this was a great disappointment.
113497.m: Scott reached the South Pole second.

113498.q: What was the name of Shackleton's ship, which was crushed by pack ice in 1915?
113498.e: The Endurance got stuck in the pack ice and was crushed by the pressure of the ice. It sank in November 1915.
113498.m: Shackleton's ship Endurance was crushed by the ice.

113499.q: On which continent did Shackleton want to land with the Endurance?
113499.e: Shackleton wanted to cross Antarctica on foot. But his ship got stuck in the pack ice before that.

113500.q: How did Shackleton's men save themselves after the Endurance sank?
113500.e: The men dragged the lifeboats across the ice and sailed them to Elephant Island. Most of them waited there for more than four months to be rescued.
113500.m: Shackleton's men saved themselves in lifeboats.

113501.q: Why did Shackleton sail across the stormy ocean in the small boat James Caird?
a: To fetch help for his men
113501.e: Shackleton and five companions sailed about 1300 kilometres to South Georgia. From a whaling station there, he organised the rescue.
113501.m: Shackleton fetched help in the James Caird.

113502.q: How many men of the Endurance's crew died?
113502.e: Even though the ship was lost, all the men of the Endurance survived. That is why Shackleton is seen as an example of good leadership in an emergency.
113502.m: All the men of the Endurance survived thanks to Shackleton's leadership.

113503.q: At what depth was the wreck of the Endurance found in 2022?
113503.e: A search expedition discovered the wreck in 2022 at a depth of about 3000 metres. It is amazingly well preserved in the cold water.
113503.m: The wreck of the Endurance lies about 3000 metres deep.

113504.q: Why did Shackleton turn back shortly before the South Pole in 1909?
a: So that his men would survive the return journey
Because someone else was already at the pole
Because he could no longer find the way
113504.e: The supplies were no longer enough to reach the pole and get back. Shackleton turned back about 180 kilometres from his goal and so saved his men.
113504.m: Shackleton turned back in 1909 so that everyone would survive.

113505.q: Which region of the Earth did Ernest Shackleton explore?
113505.e: Shackleton led several expeditions to Antarctica around the South Pole. He was born in Ireland in 1874.
113505.m: Ernest Shackleton was an Antarctic explorer.

113506.q: Which country did the polar explorer Roald Amundsen come from?
113506.e: Roald Amundsen was Norwegian. He planted the flag of Norway at the South Pole. His rival Robert Scott came from Great Britain.

113508.q: Which animals were most important for Amundsen's success?
113508.e: Amundsen's sledges were pulled by Greenland dogs. The dogs coped with cold and snow much better than other draught animals.
113508.m: With sledge dogs, Amundsen reached the South Pole quickly.

113509.q: What is the research station called that stands at the South Pole today and remembers both rivals?
113509.e: The American station at the South Pole bears the names of both polar explorers. It was founded in 1956 and is lived in all year round.
113509.m: The station at the South Pole is named after Amundsen and Scott.

113510.q: How much later than Amundsen did Scott's group arrive at the South Pole?
113510.e: Scott reached the pole on 17 January 1912, 34 days after the Norwegians. The British were bitterly disappointed.
113510.m: Scott reached the South Pole about five weeks after Amundsen.

113511.q: What did Scott and his companions find at the South Pole?
a: A tent with a letter and the flag of Norway
113511.e: Amundsen had left a tent called Polheim at the pole. Inside was a letter that Scott was supposed to take back for the King of Norway.
113511.m: At the South Pole, Scott found the Norwegians' tent.

113513.q: Which goal had Amundsen originally announced in public?
113513.e: Amundsen first planned a journey to the North Pole. When he heard that others claimed to have reached the North Pole already, he secretly changed his goal.
113513.m: Amundsen first wanted to go to the North Pole and then went to the South Pole.

113514.q: What does the 1991 Environmental Protocol to the Antarctic Treaty ban?
113514.e: The Environmental Protocol protects Antarctica as a nature reserve. Mining and any extraction of raw materials are banned, except for research.
113514.m: Mining for raw materials is banned in Antarctica.

113515.q: According to the Antarctic Treaty of 1959, what may Antarctica be used for?
a: Only for peaceful purposes such as research
113515.e: The Antarctic Treaty declares Antarctica a place for peace and science. Military bases and manoeuvres are banned there.
113515.m: Antarctica is reserved for peace and research.

113516.q: What did the Antarctic Treaty do to the territorial claims of individual countries?
a: It sold them to the UN
113516.e: Several countries claim parts of Antarctica. The treaty does not recognise these claims, but it does not cancel them either, and new claims are not allowed.
113516.m: The Antarctic Treaty freezes all territorial claims.

113517.q: What does the Antarctic Treaty expressly ban in Antarctica?
113517.e: The treaty bans nuclear explosions and the dumping of radioactive waste. This is meant to keep Antarctica free of nuclear weapons.
113517.m: Nuclear tests and nuclear waste are banned in Antarctica.

113518.q: What is meant by the ozone hole?
a: A severe thinning of the ozone layer
A hole in the ice of Antarctica
113518.e: Over Antarctica, the amount of ozone falls sharply every year. But the ozone there has not completely disappeared; it has only become very thin.
113518.m: The ozone hole is a severely thinned area of the ozone layer.

113519.q: When is the ozone hole over Antarctica at its largest each year?
113519.e: In the Antarctic spring, in September and October, sunlight returns. It sets off chemical reactions that break down the ozone especially quickly.
113519.m: The ozone hole is largest in the Antarctic spring.

113520.q: Which agreement from 1987 restricted the production of substances that damage the ozone layer?
113520.e: In the Montreal Protocol, countries agreed to ban ozone-damaging substances step by step. It is seen as one of the most successful environmental agreements.
113520.m: The Montreal Protocol protects the ozone layer.

113521.q: How many oxygen atoms does an ozone molecule consist of?
113521.e: Ozone has the chemical formula O3. Normal oxygen in the air, on the other hand, consists of two oxygen atoms.
113521.m: An ozone molecule consists of three oxygen atoms.

113522.q: In which layer of the atmosphere is the protective ozone layer?
113522.e: The ozone layer lies in the stratosphere, about 15 to 35 kilometres above the ground. The weather happens below it, in the troposphere.
113522.m: The ozone layer is in the stratosphere.

113523.q: In which year was the discovery of the ozone hole over Antarctica published?
113523.e: Researchers from the British Antarctic Survey reported the sharply reduced ozone levels in 1985. They had made the measurements at a British station in Antarctica.
113523.m: The ozone hole was made public in 1985.

113524.q: How many eggs does a female emperor penguin lay per breeding season?
113524.e: The female lays just one egg. On the ice, it would be impossible to keep several eggs warm at the same time.
113524.m: An emperor penguin lays only one egg a year.

113525.q: Roughly how tall does an adult emperor penguin grow?
113525.e: Emperor penguins grow to more than a metre tall and usually weigh 20 to 40 kilograms. That makes them about as tall as a child of nursery school age.
113525.m: An emperor penguin grows to more than a metre tall.

113526.q: Who incubates the egg in emperor penguins?
113526.e: Shortly after laying, the female hands the egg to the male and goes to the sea to feed. The male incubates the egg alone.
113526.m: In emperor penguins, the male incubates the egg.

113527.q: Where does the emperor penguin's egg lie while it is being incubated?
a: On the feet under a fold of skin
In a nest made of stones
In a cave in the snow
In the water under the ice
113527.e: The egg rests on the bird's feet and is covered by a warm fold of belly skin. This way it never touches the freezing ice.
113527.m: The emperor penguin keeps its egg warm on its feet.

113528.q: How do emperor penguins protect themselves together from icy storms?
113528.e: Thousands of birds stand close together and slowly swap places. This way, each one gets a turn in the warm middle.
113528.m: Emperor penguins keep each other warm in tight huddles.

113529.q: How deep can emperor penguins dive when hunting?
113529.e: Emperor penguins are excellent divers and reach depths of more than 500 metres. No other bird dives so deep.
113529.m: Emperor penguins dive deeper than any other bird.

113530.q: Roughly how long does the male emperor penguin incubate the egg without eating?
113530.e: Incubation lasts a good 60 days, and during this time the male eats nothing. It lives off its fat reserves and loses a lot of weight.
113530.m: A male emperor penguin fasts for about two months while incubating.

113531.q: Roughly how much of the Earth's fresh water is stored in the Antarctic ice?
113531.e: The Antarctic Ice Sheet is the largest mass of ice on Earth. It contains about 70 per cent of all fresh water.
113531.m: Most of the Earth's fresh water is in the Antarctic ice.

113532.q: How thick is the Antarctic Ice Sheet on average?
113532.e: The ice is about 2 kilometres thick on average, and almost 5 kilometres at its thickest. Under this weight, the bedrock is pressed deep down.
113532.m: The ice of Antarctica is about two kilometres thick on average.

113533.q: By how much would the sea level rise if all the Antarctic ice melted?
113533.e: Experts calculate a rise of about 58 metres. But melting completely would take many thousands of years.
113533.m: The Antarctic ice could raise the sea level by about 58 metres.

113534.q: Roughly how big is the Ross Ice Shelf, the largest ice shelf in Antarctica?
a: About as big as Lake Constance
About as big as the canton of Zurich
About as big as all of Africa
113534.e: The Ross Ice Shelf is a floating sheet of ice about the size of France. Its ice edge rises up to 50 metres out of the sea.
113534.m: The largest ice shelf is about as big as France.

a: A sheet of ice floating on the sea
A layer of hail on mountains
113535.e: An ice shelf forms when glaciers flow from the land into the sea and start to float there. It stays connected to the ice on land until big pieces break off as icebergs.
113535.m: An ice shelf is a floating sheet of ice connected to the land ice.

113536.q: What can researchers read from air bubbles in Antarctic ice cores?
a: What the air used to be made of
113536.e: Tiny air bubbles from the past are trapped in the ice. In them, scientists can measure, for example, how much carbon dioxide the air used to contain.
113536.m: Ice cores are an archive of the climate of the past.

113537.q: Which part of the Antarctic Ice Sheet is the larger one?
a: Both are exactly the same size
The ice sheet of the Antarctic Peninsula
113537.e: The East Antarctic Ice Sheet is much larger and thicker than the western one. Most of it lies on solid land above sea level.
113537.m: Most of Antarctica's ice is in East Antarctica.

113538.q: Where does the bedrock under the West Antarctic Ice Sheet lie in many places?
113538.e: Under the western ice, the rock often lies far below sea level. That is why this part is seen as especially sensitive when warm seawater gets under the ice.
113538.m: The West Antarctic ice rests on rock below sea level.

113539.e: Xavier Mertz was born in Basel in 1882. He was one of the first Swiss people to take part in a big Antarctic expedition.
113539.m: Xavier Mertz was a Swiss polar explorer.

113540.q: Where did Xavier Mertz travel with an expedition from 1911?
113540.e: Mertz took part in the expedition of the Australian Douglas Mawson. It explored an unknown stretch of the Antarctic coast.
113540.m: Xavier Mertz did research in Antarctica.

113541.q: Which animals was Xavier Mertz in charge of on the expedition?
113541.e: Mertz looked after the sledge dogs together with the Briton Belgrave Ninnis. The dogs pulled the sledges with equipment and food.
113541.m: Xavier Mertz looked after the sledge dogs.

113542.q: Which skills did Xavier Mertz bring with him from Switzerland?
a: He was a skier and mountaineer
He was a captain and navigator
He was a cook and baker
He was a pilot and mechanic
113542.e: Mertz was an experienced mountaineer and a successful skier. He had also studied law and earned a doctorate.
113542.m: Xavier Mertz was a good skier and mountaineer.

113543.q: What happened in December 1912 to Belgrave Ninnis, the companion of Mertz and Mawson?
a: He was rescued by a ship
He reached the South Pole alone
113543.e: Ninnis broke through into a deep crevasse with a sledge and dogs. A large part of the food and equipment was lost with him.
113543.m: Belgrave Ninnis disappeared into a crevasse with the supplies.

113544.q: According to what people believe today, what did Xavier Mertz die of?
a: An attack by a leopard seal
113544.e: Mertz and Mawson had to eat their dogs, including their livers. Dog liver contains a great deal of vitamin A, which is poisonous in large amounts.
113544.m: Too much vitamin A from dog liver was probably fatal for Xavier Mertz.

113545.q: What in Antarctica is named after Xavier Mertz?
113545.e: The Mertz Glacier in East Antarctica bears his name. Next to it there is also a glacier named after Ninnis.
113545.m: The Mertz Glacier remembers the polar explorer from Basel.

113546.q: Why did Mertz and Mawson have to eat their dogs on the way back?
a: They did not like any other food
113546.e: A sledge carrying most of the food fell into a crevasse with Belgrave Ninnis. Mertz died on the way back in January 1913.
113546.m: Without supplies, the explorers had to eat their dogs.

113547.q: What did Douglas Mawson miss by just a few hours after Mertz's death?
a: The departure of the expedition ship
113547.e: When Mawson reached the base camp, the ship Aurora had just left. He had to spend another winter in Antarctica with a few men.
113547.m: Mawson just missed the ship and stayed for another winter.

113548.e: McMurdo Station is a research station of the United States. It is run as part of the American Antarctic programme.
113548.m: McMurdo Station belongs to the USA.

113549.q: What is special about the size of McMurdo Station?
a: It is the largest station in Antarctica
It is the smallest station in Antarctica
It is exactly at the South Pole
113549.e: McMurdo is like a small village with houses, laboratories, workshops and runways. No other station in Antarctica is bigger.
113549.m: McMurdo is the largest research station in Antarctica.

113550.q: How do people and supplies usually get to McMurdo Station in Antarctica?
113550.e: The station is on Ross Island at the edge of Antarctica. It is supplied by aeroplanes that land on ice runways, and by ships in the southern summer.
113550.m: McMurdo is supplied by aeroplane and ship.

113551.q: Roughly how many people live at McMurdo Station in summer?
113551.e: In the southern summer, more than 1000 people work at the station. In winter, only a few hundred stay.
113551.m: In summer, more than a thousand people live at McMurdo Station.

113552.q: From which country do many supply flights to McMurdo Station take off?
113552.e: Most flights to McMurdo take off from Christchurch in New Zealand, which is the closest to the station. The planes land on runways of ice and snow.
113552.m: Many flights to McMurdo Station take off in New Zealand.

113553.q: Which station of another country is only a few kilometres from McMurdo?
113553.e: New Zealand's Scott Base is only about three kilometres from McMurdo. The two stations work closely together.
113553.m: New Zealand's Scott Base is next to McMurdo.

113554.q: Which active volcano rises near McMurdo Station?
113554.e: Mount Erebus on Ross Island is the southernmost active volcano on Earth. There is a lava lake in its crater.
113554.m: The active volcano Mount Erebus stands near McMurdo.

113555.q: How was McMurdo Station partly supplied with electricity from 1962 to 1972?
113555.e: A small nuclear reactor supplied electricity and heat for ten years. Because of problems, it was taken down and the contaminated soil was removed.
113555.m: McMurdo once had its own small nuclear reactor.

113556.e: Krill are shrimp-like crustaceans that live in huge swarms in the sea. Antarctic krill is the best-known kind.
113556.m: Krill are small crustaceans that live in swarms.

113557.q: What does Antarctic krill mainly feed on?
113557.e: Krill filter tiny plant plankton out of the water. In winter they also graze algae from the underside of the sea ice.
113557.m: Krill eat tiny algae in the sea.

113558.q: Which largest animal on Earth feeds mainly on krill?
113558.e: The blue whale filters huge amounts of krill out of the water with its baleen plates. It can eat several tonnes in a day.
113558.m: The huge blue whale eats tiny krill.

113559.q: Which seal, despite its name, feeds almost only on krill?
113559.e: The crabeater seal has special teeth that it uses like a sieve to filter krill out of the water. It hardly eats crabs at all.
113559.m: The crabeater seal is really a krill eater.

113560.q: Roughly how big does an Antarctic krill grow?
113560.e: Adult Antarctic krill grow to about 6 centimetres long. That is about as long as a little finger.
113560.m: Antarctic krill grow about as long as a little finger.

113561.q: What special ability does krill have thanks to its light organs?
113561.e: Krill have small light organs on their bodies. They can use them to glow faintly, probably to communicate within the swarm.
113561.m: Krill can make light with their light organs.

113562.q: What is krill mainly fished for?
a: For fish food and krill oil
113562.e: Krill is made into feed for fish farms and into oil for food supplements. The amounts caught are limited internationally.
113562.m: Krill is mainly caught for animal feed and oil.

113563.q: Why is krill so important for life in the Southern Ocean?
a: Many animals depend on it for food
It cleans dirt off the ice
It produces most of the oxygen
113563.e: Whales, seals, penguins, fish and seabirds eat krill. Without it, the food web of Antarctica would collapse.
113563.m: Krill is a cornerstone of the food web in Antarctica.

a: A lake under the ice of Antarctica
A crater lake on the moon
113564.e: Lake Vostok is a huge lake hidden under the thick ice of East Antarctica. Lakes like this are called subglacial lakes.
113564.m: Lake Vostok lies hidden under the Antarctic ice.

113565.q: Roughly how thick is the ice above Lake Vostok?
113565.e: Above the lake there is a layer of ice about 3700 to 4000 metres thick. That is why the lake remained undiscovered for a long time.
113565.m: Lake Vostok lies under about four kilometres of ice.

113566.q: Why did researchers drill down to Lake Vostok especially carefully?
a: So that the lake water would not be polluted
So that the lake would not drain
So that the ice would not melt
So that the fish would not be frightened
113566.e: The lake had been cut off from the outside world for a very long time. Foreign substances and bacteria from the borehole could contaminate it. The water was first reached in 2012.
113566.m: Lake Vostok should stay clean during drilling.

113567.q: Why is the water of Lake Vostok liquid despite the cold?
a: Because of the pressure of the ice and heat from inside the Earth
Because it contains a lot of salt
113567.e: The heavy ice presses hard on the lake, so the water only freezes below 0 degrees. On top of that, heat from inside the Earth warms it from below.
113567.m: Pressure and heat from the Earth keep Lake Vostok liquid.

113568.q: Which record does Lake Vostok hold among the lakes under the ice of Antarctica?
113568.e: Of the several hundred known lakes under the Antarctic ice, Lake Vostok is the largest. It is about 250 kilometres long.
113568.m: Lake Vostok is the largest lake under the ice of Antarctica.

113569.q: What does the Russian word “Vostok”, after which the lake is named, mean?
113569.e: The lake is named after the station above it, which in turn is named after a ship of the explorer Bellingshausen. “Vostok” is Russian for east.
113569.m: The Russian word Vostok means east.

113570.q: Which country runs the research station above Lake Vostok?
113570.e: Vostok Station was founded by the Soviet Union in 1957. Today it is run by Russia.
113570.m: There is a Russian station above Lake Vostok.

113571.q: Roughly how big is the area of Lake Vostok?
113571.e: The lake has an area of about 12,500 square kilometres. That is more than twenty times the size of Lake Geneva.
113571.m: Lake Vostok is more than twenty times the size of Lake Geneva.

113572.q: Why are space researchers also interested in Lake Vostok?
a: It is similar to seas under the ice of Jupiter's moons
It is used as a landing site for rockets
It reflects the stars especially well
113572.e: Jupiter's moon Europa probably has an ocean under a crust of ice. Life in Lake Vostok would show that life is possible in places like that too.
113572.m: Lake Vostok helps in the search for life on icy moons.

113573.q: A 9-volt battery drives a current of 0.5 amps through a small bulb. What is the resistance?
113573.e: Resistance is voltage divided by current. 9 V / 0.5 A makes 18 Ω.
113573.m: You get resistance from voltage divided by current.

113574.q: 2 amps flow through a resistance of 6 ohms. What voltage is applied?
113574.e: Voltage is resistance times current. 6 Ω × 2 A makes 12 V.
113574.m: You get voltage from resistance times current.

113575.q: What does the graph of current against voltage look like for an ohmic resistor?
a: A straight line through the origin
113575.e: Because current and voltage are proportional, all the measured points lie on a straight line. It starts at the origin, because without voltage no current flows.
113575.m: For an ohmic resistor, the measurements give a straight line through the origin.

113576.q: Suppose a human body has a resistance of 1000 ohms. How big would the current be at 230 volts?
113576.e: 230 V / 1000 Ω makes 0.23 A, which is 230 milliamps. Even much smaller currents can kill a person.
113576.m: Even the voltage from a socket can drive a deadly current through the body.

113577.q: A 4.5-volt flat battery is connected to a resistance of 15 ohms. How big is the current?
113577.e: You work out 4.5 V / 15 Ω. That makes 0.3 A.
113577.m: With Ohm's law you can work out any of the three quantities.

113578.q: A small bulb with a resistance of 12 ohms is connected to a voltage of 6 volts. How big is the current?
113578.e: You divide the voltage by the resistance. 6 V / 12 Ω makes 0.5 A.
113578.m: If the resistance in ohms is bigger than the voltage in volts, less than one amp flows.

113579.q: What resistance is needed for exactly 2 amps to flow at 230 volts?
113579.e: Resistance is voltage divided by current. 230 V / 2 A makes 115 Ω.
113579.m: With Ohm's law you can work out the right resistance.

113580.q: What happens to the current if you halve the resistance at the same voltage?
113580.e: According to Ohm's law, current is voltage divided by resistance. If the number you divide by becomes half as big, the result becomes twice as big.
113580.m: A smaller resistance lets more current flow at the same voltage.

113581.q: Which formula symbol is used for electrical resistance?
113581.e: The R comes from the Latin word resistere, which means to resist. U stands for voltage and I for current.
113581.m: Electrical resistance has the formula symbol R.

113582.q: How does the resistance change if you use a thicker wire made of the same metal?
113582.e: A thicker wire offers the current a larger cross-section. So its resistance falls.
113582.m: The thicker a wire, the smaller its resistance.

113583.q: What usually happens to the resistance of a metal wire when it gets hot?
113583.e: In a hot metal the atoms vibrate more strongly. The electrons are slowed down more often, and the resistance rises.
113583.m: In metals, resistance rises with temperature.

113584.q: What are materials called whose resistance disappears completely at very low temperatures?
113584.e: Below a certain very low temperature, superconductors conduct electricity with no resistance at all. They are used, for example, for strong magnets in hospitals and particle accelerators.
113584.m: Superconductors have no resistance at very low temperatures.

113585.q: What is the resistance of the heating element in a kettle for?
113585.e: When current flows through a resistance, electrical energy is turned into heat. The heating element gets hot and warms the water.
113585.m: A heating element uses resistance to produce heat.

113586.q: Two resistors of 100 ohms each are connected in parallel. What is the total resistance?
113586.e: In a parallel circuit the current has two paths and gets through more easily. Two equal resistors together give half, so 100 Ω / 2 equals 50 Ω.
113586.m: Resistors in parallel give a smaller total resistance.

113587.q: What is a component called whose resistance you can adjust with a knob?
113587.e: A potentiometer is an adjustable resistor. It is found, for example, in old volume controls or dimmers.
113587.m: With a potentiometer you can adjust the resistance.

113588.q: Which Greek letter is the symbol for the unit ohm?
113588.e: The ohm is abbreviated with the capital Greek omega, which looks like this: Ω. This way it is not confused with the digit 0.
113588.m: The symbol for ohm is the Greek omega.

113589.q: What did Georg Simon Ohm, after whom the unit ohm is named, study?
a: How voltage and current are related
How light is refracted in glass
113589.e: Ohm found that in a wire the current grows in the same proportion as the voltage. He published this in 1827; today it is called Ohm's law.
113589.m: The unit ohm honours the physicist Georg Simon Ohm.

113590.q: Which quantity is measured in ohms?
113590.e: Resistance tells you how strongly a component holds back the current. Voltage is measured in volts, current in amps and power in watts.
113590.m: Electrical resistance is measured in ohms.

113591.q: What resistance does a component have if exactly 1 amp flows through it at 1 volt?
113591.e: One ohm is defined as one volt per amp. 1 V / 1 A makes exactly 1 Ω.
113591.m: One ohm equals one volt per amp.

113592.m: One kilohm is a thousand ohms.

113593.e: Mega means a million. 2 × 1,000,000 makes 2,000,000 Ω.
113593.m: One megohm is a million ohms.

113594.q: Which instrument can you use to measure a resistance in ohms?
113594.e: A multimeter can measure voltage, current and resistance. To measure resistance you set it to the ohm range.
113594.m: Resistances are measured with a multimeter.

113595.q: What do the coloured rings on small resistors in electronics show?
113595.e: Each colour stands for a digit or a multiplier. This lets you read the value even on tiny components.
113595.m: The colour rings reveal the value of a resistor.

113597.q: Why do metals conduct electricity well?
113597.e: In metals some electrons are not tightly bound to an atom. These free electrons can move and so carry the current.
113597.m: Free electrons make metals good conductors.

113598.q: What is the insulation around the wires of an electric cable usually made of?
113598.e: Plastic is an insulator and lets almost no current through. The covering protects against touching the live wires.
113598.m: Plastic insulates the wires in cables.

113600.q: Why does ordinary tap water conduct electricity?
a: Because salts are dissolved in it
Because it comes from the mountains
113600.e: Tap water contains dissolved mineral salts that form charged particles. That is why water and electrical appliances are dangerous together.

113601.q: Which substance in a pencil lead conducts electricity?
113601.e: Pencil leads are made of graphite and clay; they contain no lead. Graphite is a form of carbon that conducts electricity.
113601.m: Graphite in pencil leads is an electrical conductor.

113602.e: Silver has the lowest resistivity of all metals, just ahead of copper. Because it is expensive, it is only rarely used for cables.
113602.m: Silver is the best metallic conductor.

113604.q: Is dry air normally an electrical conductor or an insulator?
113604.e: Dry air normally lets hardly any current through. Only at very high voltage, as with lightning, can a current pass through the air.
113604.m: Air insulates as long as the voltage is not extremely high.

113605.q: Why is a short circuit dangerous?
a: The wires heat up strongly and can catch fire
The voltage falls to zero and everything gets cold
113605.e: Because of the very large current, the wires get hot. Without protection the insulation can melt and a fire can start.
113605.m: The great heat of a short circuit can start a fire.

113606.q: What is a common cause of a short circuit?
a: A lamp that is too bright
113606.e: If a cable's insulation is damaged, the wires can touch. Then the current flows directly from one conductor to the other.
113606.m: Damaged cables are a common cause of short circuits.

113607.q: How big is the resistance of the circuit in a short circuit?
113607.e: In a short circuit the resistance of the device is missing; only the small resistance of the wires remains. According to Ohm's law the current then becomes huge.
113607.m: In a short circuit the resistance is very small and the current very large.

113608.q: In a short circuit at 230 volts the resistance is only 0.5 ohms. What current would flow?
113608.e: You work out 230 V / 0.5 Ω. That makes 460 A, many times the normal current in a household wire.
113608.m: A tiny resistance leads to a huge short-circuit current.

113609.q: What can be seen at the fault point in a short circuit?
113609.e: The large current can heat the air at the fault point so much that it glows. This produces sparks or a bright electric arc.
113609.m: A short circuit can produce sparks and electric arcs.

113610.q: Which device in the house automatically cuts off the current in a short circuit?
113610.e: The fuse detects the excessive current and breaks the circuit. This prevents a fire.
113610.m: In a short circuit the fuse trips.

113611.q: Why should you not carry loose batteries in your pocket together with keys or coins?
a: The metal can short-circuit the terminals
113611.e: If a piece of metal touches both terminals at once, a short circuit occurs. The battery can get hot and in the worst case catch fire.
113611.m: Metal in your pocket can short-circuit a battery.

113612.q: When a standard lamp is switched on, the fuse trips immediately. What is the most likely cause?
a: A short circuit in the lamp
A bulb that is too weak
Too little voltage in the mains
113612.e: If the fuse trips exactly when a device is switched on, a very large current is suddenly flowing there. Usually a short circuit in the device or cable is to blame, and it should be checked.
113612.m: If the fuse trips when you switch on, a short circuit in the device is often to blame.

113613.q: How does a cartridge fuse work?
a: A thin wire melts if the current is too high
A magnet pulls out the plug
113613.e: A cartridge fuse contains a thin fuse wire. If the current gets too big, it gets so hot that it melts and breaks the circuit.
113613.m: In a cartridge fuse a thin wire melts if there is too much current.

113614.q: What must you do after a cartridge fuse has blown?
a: Replace it with a new one
113614.e: The fuse wire is destroyed when the fuse blows. So the fuse must be replaced with a new one of the same rating.
113614.m: A blown cartridge fuse must be replaced.

113615.q: What does a fuse in the house mainly protect against?
a: Electricity bills that are too high
113615.e: The fuse switches off if too much current flows through a wire. This stops the cables getting too hot and prevents a fire.
113615.m: Fuses protect the wires from overheating.

113616.q: What is the advantage of a circuit breaker over a cartridge fuse?
a: You can switch it back on
It lets much more current through
