113616.e: A circuit breaker switches off when there is too much current. Once the fault has been fixed, you simply flip the lever back.
113616.m: A circuit breaker can be switched back on after it trips.

113617.q: In which unit is the rating on a fuse given?
113617.e: A fuse shows the current at which it still does not trip over time, for example 10 A. If much more current flows, it switches off.
113617.m: Fuses are rated by current in amps.

113618.q: Why must you never bridge a blown fuse with a piece of wire?
a: Because there would then be no protection against overheating
Because the wire conducts too little current
Because the fuse would otherwise cost more
113618.e: A thick wire does not melt when the current is too high. The wires can then overheat and cause a fire.
113618.m: A fuse must never be bridged with wire.

113619.q: What can happen if you fit a fuse with too high an amp rating?
a: The wires can overheat before it trips
113619.e: A fuse that is too big lets through more current than the wire can take. The cables can get hot and cause a fire before the fuse switches off.
113619.m: A fuse must match the wire.

113620.q: Where are the fuses in a house?
113620.e: In the fuse box, also called the consumer unit, each circuit has its own fuse. There you can switch off individual parts of the home.
113620.m: A house's fuses are in the fuse box.

113621.q: What does a residual current device constantly compare?
a: The current flowing out with the current flowing back
The voltage with the time of day
The electricity price with the usage
113621.e: Normally the same amount of current flows to the device as flows back. If some is missing, it is flowing away somewhere else, and the device trips.
113621.m: An RCD notices when current takes a wrong path.

113622.q: At what fault current does an RCD for protecting people typically trip?
113622.e: RCDs for protecting people trip at a fault current of 30 milliamps at the latest. That is much less than an ordinary fuse needs.
113622.m: To protect people, an RCD trips at 30 milliamps.

113623.e: Milli means one thousandth. 30 divided by 1000 makes 0.03 A.
113623.m: One milliamp is a thousandth of an amp.

113624.q: How quickly does an RCD switch off when there is a fault?
a: In a fraction of a second
113624.e: An RCD cuts the circuit within fractions of a second. This keeps the time in which current flows through a body very short.
113624.m: An RCD switches off in a flash.

113625.q: What should you do with the test button of an RCD?
a: Press it regularly to test that it works
Keep it pressed all the time
113625.e: Pressing the test button imitates a fault current. If the RCD switches off, it is working properly.
113625.m: The test button shows whether the RCD still works.

a: Current that flows to earth by a wrong path
Current that stands still in the cable
113626.e: A fault current does not flow back through the intended wire, but, for example, through a casing or a person into the earth. That is exactly what the safety switch detects.
113626.m: A fault current takes a wrong path, often through the earth.

113627.q: What is the residual current device often called for short in Switzerland?
113627.e: F stands for Fehlerstrom (fault current) and I for the formula symbol of current. An LS switch, on the other hand, is a circuit breaker. In English it is usually called an RCD.
113627.m: In Switzerland the RCD is called an FI switch for short.

113628.q: Where is an RCD especially important because the risk of electric shock is higher there?
a: In the bedroom and the attic
In the stairwell and the cellar
In the office and the living room
113628.e: Where there is water and damp, the body has a good connection to the earth. An RCD can save lives there in an accident.
113628.m: Where it is wet, an RCD protects especially well.

113629.q: What does earthing mean in electrical engineering?
a: A conducting connection to the ground
113629.e: In earthing, part of the installation is connected to the ground by a conductor. This lets current flow safely into the earth if there is a fault.
113629.m: Earthing connects an installation to the ground by a conductor.

113630.q: What is a lightning conductor on a house for?
a: It carries the lightning current safely into the earth
It draws thunderstorms away from the house
It stores the energy of the lightning
113630.e: If lightning strikes, the current flows through the rod and thick cables into the ground. So the house is not damaged.
113630.m: A lightning conductor carries lightning current into the earth.

113631.q: What is a foundation earth electrode?
a: A metal strip in the concrete foundation of a building
A cable in the roof space
113631.e: During construction a metal strip is laid in the foundation. Through the concrete it has good contact with the earth and serves as earthing for the whole house.
113631.m: The foundation earth electrode earths the whole building through its foundation.

113632.q: Why are the metal casings of many devices earthed?
a: So that fault current doesn't flow through people
So that the devices use less electricity
So that they warm up faster
113632.e: If a faulty wire touches the casing, the current flows away through the earth. This makes the protective device switch off before anyone gets an electric shock.
113632.m: Earthing carries dangerous currents past people.

113633.q: What does equipotential bonding in a house connect?
a: Metal parts such as water and heating pipes
The electricity bills of all the flats
113633.e: In equipotential bonding, conductive parts such as pipes are connected to each other and to the earthing. So there is no dangerous voltage between them.
113633.m: Equipotential bonding prevents voltages between metal parts.

113634.q: Why is it especially dangerous to touch a faulty device while barefoot on a wet floor?
a: Because the body is then well connected to the earth
Because the device then gives more light
113634.e: Wet skin and a wet floor have a small resistance. Current can then easily flow through the body into the earth.
113634.m: On a wet floor, current flows through the body especially easily.

113635.q: What voltage does the earth have as a reference point in electrical engineering?
113635.e: The earth counts as the reference point with 0 volts. All other voltages in an installation are given relative to this point.
113635.m: As a reference point, the earth has zero voltage.

113636.q: Why is a tanker lorry earthed while it is being filled with petrol?
a: So that no dangerous charge builds up
So that the petrol flows faster
So that the tank doesn't rust
113636.e: When fuel is transferred, electric charge can build up. A spark could ignite the petrol fumes, so the charge is carried away through the earthing.
113636.m: Earthing prevents dangerous sparks when transferring petrol.

113637.q: What colour is the protective earth wire in an electric cable?
113637.e: The protective earth wire has green and yellow stripes everywhere in the world. This colour must not be used for any other wire.
113637.m: The earth wire is always green and yellow.

113638.q: Which part of a device is the protective earth wire connected to?
113638.e: The protective earth wire connects the touchable metal casing to the earthing. If there is a fault, the current flows away through it.
113638.m: The earth wire is connected to the metal casing of a device.

113639.q: What colour is the neutral wire in a household installation?
113639.e: The neutral wire is blue. In normal use the current flows back from the device through it.

113640.q: What colour is the live wire, which carries the voltage, usually in an appliance cable?
113640.e: The live wire, often also called the phase, is usually brown in appliance cables. In installations, black and grey are also used.
113640.m: The live wire is usually brown.

113641.q: How many pins does a Swiss mains plug with a protective earth have?
113641.e: The Swiss plug with a protective earth has three pins. The middle pin, which is slightly offset, is connected to the earth wire.
113641.m: The Swiss plug with an earth has three pins.

113642.q: Why do double-insulated devices of protection class II not need an earth wire?
a: Because the live parts are covered twice
Because they are only used outdoors
Because they are always switched off
113642.e: These devices have extra insulation built in, for example a plastic casing. You can recognise them by the symbol of two squares, one inside the other.
113642.m: Double-insulated devices manage without an earth wire.

113643.q: What happens if, in a device with an earth wire, a live wire touches the metal casing?
a: The current flows away through the earth wire and the fuse trips
The device simply keeps running as usual
The voltage in the whole house rises
113643.e: Through the earth wire, a short circuit to earth with a large current occurs. This makes the protective device switch off the circuit.
113643.m: The earth wire makes sure the power is cut when there is a fault.

113644.q: What is the danger if the earth wire of a device with a metal casing is broken and a fault occurs?
a: The casing gets cold at once
113644.e: Without an earth wire the fault current cannot flow away. Anyone who touches the casing can then become the path for the current themselves.
113644.m: Without an earth wire, a faulty casing can be deadly.

113645.q: How many pins does an ordinary earthed Swiss plug have?
113645.e: The earthed Swiss plug has three round pins. They are for the live wire, the neutral wire and the earth wire.
113645.m: An earthed Swiss plug has three pins.

113646.q: Why doesn't a German Schuko plug fit into a Swiss socket?
a: It is too wide and round
113646.e: The Schuko plug has a round body with earth contacts on the sides. It is too big for the narrow Swiss socket, so you need an adapter.
113646.m: In Switzerland you need an adapter for German Schuko plugs.

113647.q: What shape is the body of a Swiss type 12 plug?
113647.e: The Swiss plug has a flat, hexagonal body. This lets it fit exactly into the matching recess of the socket.
113647.m: The Swiss plug has a hexagonal shape.

113648.q: Which pin of the three-pin Swiss plug is the earth?
a: The middle pin, which is slightly offset
113648.e: The earth pin is in the middle and is slightly offset from the line of the other two pins. This means the plug can only be put in the right way round.
113648.m: On the Swiss plug the middle pin is the earth.

113649.q: What current are ordinary Swiss type 13 sockets designed for?
113649.e: Normal household sockets are built for at most 10 amps. For bigger currents there are sockets with square pins for 16 amps.
113649.m: Normal Swiss sockets are designed for 10 amps.

113650.q: Which neighbouring country of Switzerland also uses the type J plug system?
113650.e: Liechtenstein uses the same plugs and sockets as Switzerland. In the other neighbouring countries Schuko or French plugs are usual.
113650.m: Liechtenstein also uses Swiss type J plugs.

113651.q: What is the earth wire, in other words the middle pin of the Swiss plug, for?
a: It safely carries the current away if there is a fault
It just holds the plug in place
113651.e: If a wire inside the device touches the metal casing, the current flows away through the earth wire. The fuse trips, and you don't get an electric shock.
113651.m: The earth wire protects against electric shocks.

113652.q: How many pins does the Swiss type 11 plug have?
113652.e: Type 11 is a two-pin plug without an earth. It is used for double-insulated devices.
113652.m: The Swiss type 11 plug has only two pins.

113653.q: What kind of current does a household socket supply?
113653.e: With alternating current the current keeps changing direction. Batteries, on the other hand, supply direct current, which always flows the same way.

113654.q: What voltage does an ordinary socket in Switzerland supply?
113654.e: Swiss household sockets supply 230 volts alternating voltage. Large appliances such as cookers sometimes even use 400 volts.

113655.q: From what alternating voltage is touching generally considered dangerous?
113655.e: Alternating voltages up to 50 volts count as extra-low voltage; above that, touching is dangerous. The 230 volts from a socket are far above that.
113655.m: Alternating voltages above 50 volts can kill.

113656.q: A kettle has a power of 2300 watts and runs on 230 volts. What current flows?
113656.e: Power is voltage times current. So 2300 W / 230 V gives a current of 10 A.
113656.m: Current is power divided by voltage.

113657.q: What does a mobile phone charger do with the 230-volt mains voltage?
a: It converts it into a small direct voltage
It passes it unchanged into the phone
113657.e: The charger turns the mains voltage into a small direct voltage, usually 5 volts for USB. This lets the battery be charged safely.
113657.m: A charger turns 230 volts into a small direct voltage.

113658.q: What mains voltage is usual in homes in the USA?
113658.e: In North America sockets supply around 120 volts. Travellers therefore have to check whether their devices can handle both voltages.
113658.m: In the USA the mains voltage is lower than in Europe.

113659.q: A hairdryer has a power of 1150 watts and runs on 230 volts. What current flows?
113659.e: Current is power divided by voltage. 1150 W / 230 V makes 5 A.
113659.m: You can work out the current from power and voltage.

113660.q: What does “230 V” on a device's rating plate mean?
a: The device is built for a 230-volt mains supply
The device needs 230 watts of power
The device lasts 230 hours of use
113660.e: The rating plate gives the voltage a device is built for. A device for 230 volts suits the Swiss power grid.
113660.m: The rating plate says what voltage a device is built for.

113661.q: Why is even getting close to a railway overhead line deadly?
a: The current can jump across as an electric arc
The line pulls people in magnetically
113661.e: At very high voltage, the current can jump through the air without you touching the line. So you must always keep a long distance away.
113661.m: Never get close to an overhead line, even without touching it.

113662.q: Is an overhead line live when no train is running?
a: No, only when a train is coming
113662.e: Overhead lines are switched on all the time, even when no train can be seen. So you must always treat them as deadly.
113662.m: An overhead line is always live.

113663.q: Why must you never climb onto parked goods wagons?
a: Because you get too close to the overhead line
Because the wagons have just been painted
Because the wagons start moving at once
Because the roof is made of glass
113663.e: On the roof of a wagon you are only a short distance from the overhead line. Again and again young people are badly injured or killed by an electric shock doing this.
113663.m: Climbing on railway wagons is deadly because of the overhead line.

113664.q: Why doesn't a bird on a single power line get an electric shock?
a: Because there is hardly any voltage between its feet
Because its feathers store the electricity
Because the line carries no current
113664.e: Both feet are on the same line, so the voltage difference between them is tiny. It only becomes dangerous if it touches something at another potential at the same time, for example a pylon.
113664.m: Current only flows when there is a voltage difference.

113665.q: What is the part on the roof of a locomotive that collects current from the overhead line called?
113665.e: The pantograph presses a contact strip up against the contact wire from below. This is how the current gets into the locomotive.
113665.m: A pantograph collects current from the overhead line.

113666.q: By what route does the railway current flow back from the locomotive?
113666.e: The current flows through the wheels into the rails and from there back to the substation. So the rails are part of the circuit.
113666.m: On the railway, the rails serve as the return conductor.

113667.q: Where does a large part of the SBB's railway electricity come from?
a: From its own hydroelectric power stations
113667.e: The SBB runs its own hydroelectric power stations in the Alps. There it produces a large part of the electricity for its trains itself.
113667.m: The SBB produces much of its railway electricity with its own hydropower.

113668.q: Why should you never fly kites near railway or power lines?
a: The string can carry the current to a person
The kite is attracted by the electricity
The wind is too weak there
The line cuts through the string
113668.e: If the string touches a line or comes too close to it, current can flow through the string, especially if it is damp. That can be fatal.
113668.m: Keep kites far away from power lines.

113669.q: Is a tram's overhead line harmless because it has a lower voltage than the railway's?
a: Yes, but only in dry weather
113669.e: Trams do run on a lower voltage than trains, usually around 600 volts. But that is still far more than enough to kill a person.
113669.m: A tram's overhead line also carries a dangerously high voltage.

113670.q: Which alloy consists mainly of copper and tin?
113670.e: Bronze is an alloy of copper and tin. It was so important that a whole period of prehistory is named after it.
113670.m: Bronze is a mixture of copper and tin.

113671.q: Which golden-yellow alloy is made from copper and zinc?
113671.e: Brass is made of copper and zinc. It is used, for example, for door handles, screws and brass instruments.
113671.m: Brass is made of copper and zinc.

113672.q: Which element is mixed into iron to make steel?
113672.e: Steel is iron with a small amount of carbon, usually less than 2 per cent. The carbon makes the iron harder and stronger.
113672.m: Steel is iron with a little carbon.

113673.q: Which material has the highest value of 10 on the Mohs hardness scale?
113673.e: Diamond is the hardest natural mineral and has a value of 10 on the Mohs scale. Quartz has 7, topaz 8 and corundum 9.
113673.m: Diamond is the hardest mineral on the Mohs scale.

113674.q: What does the density of a material tell you?
113674.e: Density is the mass of a substance divided by its volume. Lead, for example, has a much higher density than wood.
113674.m: Density tells you how much mass there is in a certain volume.

113675.q: Which metal is usually used for electric cables because it conducts electricity so well?
113675.e: Copper conducts electricity very well and is affordable. That is why most electric cables in the home are made of copper wire.
113675.m: Copper is the typical metal for electric cables.

113676.q: On which metal does reddish-brown rust form in damp air?
113676.e: Rust forms when iron reacts with oxygen and water. Copper, on the other hand, forms a green layer, and gold does not rust at all.
113676.m: Rust forms when iron reacts with oxygen and water.

a: A material made of several materials firmly joined together
A metal that is especially pure
A plastic made of just one kind
A stone that has grown naturally
113677.e: A composite consists of two or more materials that are firmly joined together. Together it has better properties than each material on its own.
113677.m: A composite combines the strengths of several materials.

113678.q: Which two materials make up reinforced concrete?
113678.e: In reinforced concrete, steel bars, called reinforcement, are cast into the concrete. This makes a very strong building material for bridges and houses.
113678.m: Reinforced concrete has steel inside the concrete.

113679.q: What holds the fibres together in fibre-reinforced plastic?
113679.e: The fibres are embedded in a synthetic resin that protects them and holds them together. Experts call this material the matrix.
113679.m: Synthetic resin holds the fibres together in a composite.

113680.q: Which natural material counts as a composite made of fibres and a binding substance?
113680.e: Wood consists of cellulose fibres held together by lignin. That makes it a natural fibre composite.
113680.m: Wood is a natural composite material.

113681.q: What was once mixed into mud bricks so that they cracked less as they dried?
113681.e: The straws act like fibres and hold the mud together. This is a very old form of composite material.

113682.q: What is the main job of the steel in reinforced concrete?
113682.e: Concrete copes very well with pressure but cracks easily when it is pulled. The steel bars take up these pulling forces.
113682.m: Concrete takes pressure and steel takes pulling.

113683.q: What are the rotor blades of wind turbines usually made of?
113683.e: Rotor blades have to be light, stiff and very long. That is why they are usually built from plastic reinforced with glass or carbon fibres.
113683.m: Wind turbine blades are usually made of fibre-reinforced plastic.

113684.q: Which abbreviation stands for carbon fibre reinforced plastic?
113684.e: CFRP stands for carbon fibre reinforced plastic. In everyday language, people often just say “carbon”.
113684.m: CFRP is plastic reinforced with carbon fibres.

113685.e: Carbon fibres are made almost entirely of carbon and are therefore black, like coal or graphite. That is why carbon bike frames often look black.

113686.q: How are the starting fibres turned into carbon fibres?
a: By heating them strongly without oxygen
By shining UV light on them
113686.e: The fibres are heated to very high temperatures with no air. Almost all the other elements escape, and carbon is left.
113686.m: Carbon fibres are made by strong heating without oxygen.

113687.q: How thick is a single carbon fibre compared with a human hair?
113687.e: A carbon fibre is only about 7 micrometres thick, and a hair is about ten times thicker. That is why thousands of fibres are gathered into bundles.
113687.m: A carbon fibre is much thinner than a hair.

113688.q: Why are carbon fibres valued in building aeroplanes and bikes?
a: They are very strong and light at the same time
They are soft and stretch easily
113688.e: Parts made of CFRP are very strong and stiff but much lighter than steel ones. Lighter vehicles need less energy.
113688.m: Carbon fibres are strong and light at the same time.

113689.q: Which Swiss solar aeroplane flew around the Earth in 2015 and 2016 and had a structure made of carbon fibre composite?
113689.e: Solar Impulse 2, flown by Bertrand Piccard and André Borschberg, flew around the world on solar energy alone. To manage this, the plane had to be built extremely light.
113689.m: Solar Impulse 2 flew around the world on solar energy alone.

113690.q: Which property makes carbon fibres different from glass fibres?
113690.e: Carbon conducts electricity, while glass is an insulator. That is why you have to think about electrical conductivity with CFRP parts.
113690.m: Carbon fibres conduct electricity, glass fibres do not.

113691.q: What does an aeroplane save if it is built largely from carbon fibre plastic instead of metal?
113691.e: Parts made of carbon fibre plastic are lighter than metal ones. A lighter plane needs less fuel. In the Boeing 787, about half of the structure is made of it.

113692.q: What did Thomas Edison use carbonised fibres of bamboo or cotton for around 1880?
113692.e: Edison made carbonised fibres glow in his light bulbs. This is seen as an early use of carbon fibres.
113692.m: Early light bulbs glowed with carbonised fibres.

113693.q: What job did the person who invented Kevlar have?
113693.e: The chemist Stephanie Kwolek discovered the fibre while researching light tyres. She received many awards for her invention.
113693.m: Kevlar was invented by a chemist.

113694.q: What kind of fibre is Kevlar?
113694.e: Kevlar was developed in a laboratory in 1965 and is made in factories. It does not occur in nature.

113695.q: Apart from protective vests, where else is Kevlar used?
a: In strong ropes and sports boats
113695.e: Kevlar is light and very hard to tear. That is why it is also found in ropes, canoes, helmets and bike tyres.
113695.m: Kevlar makes many things light and tear-resistant.

113696.q: Which piece of protective equipment is Kevlar especially known for?
113696.e: Several layers of Kevlar fabric can slow down bullets and fragments. That is why it is used in police protective vests.
113696.m: Kevlar is used in protective vests.

113697.q: For the same weight, roughly how much stronger under tension than steel is Kevlar?
113697.e: For the same weight, Kevlar is about five times as strong under tension as steel. So it is very strong and still light.
113697.m: For the same weight, Kevlar is much stronger under tension than steel.

113698.q: What do Kevlar fibres need to be protected from, because otherwise they lose strength?
113698.e: Aramid fibres are damaged by ultraviolet light from the sun. That is why in products they are usually covered or coated.

113699.q: What colour are untreated Kevlar fibres typically?
113699.e: Kevlar is naturally golden yellow. This is often how you can recognise it in fabrics.

113700.q: Which work clothing often contains Kevlar because it resists cuts?
113700.e: Kevlar is very hard to cut through with knives. That is why it is used in gloves and in cut-resistant trousers for working with a chainsaw.

113701.q: Which two properties make Gore-Tex so popular for rain jackets?
113701.e: Gore-Tex does not let rain in, but it lets moisture from the body out. So you get wet neither from the outside nor from the inside.

113702.q: What is between the outer and inner fabric of a Gore-Tex jacket?
a: A thin membrane with tiny pores
113702.e: The membrane is a very thin plastic skin with countless tiny holes. It lets vapour out but no rain in.
113702.m: A membrane with pores makes Gore-Tex waterproof.

113703.q: What are Gore-Tex fabrics mainly used for?
a: For rain jackets and hiking boots
113703.e: Gore-Tex keeps out rain and lets sweat out as vapour. That is why it is used in a lot of outdoor clothing and shoes.
113703.m: Gore-Tex protects you from getting wet outdoors.

113704.q: Why can raindrops not get through the membrane, while water vapour can?
a: The pores are smaller than drops but bigger than vapour particles
The membrane soaks up the water
The membrane is heated on the inside
113704.e: The pores are far too small for liquid drops of water. But single particles of water vapour fit through.
113704.m: The tiny pores let vapour through, but not drops.

113705.q: Which objects in the kitchen are often coated with the same plastic as the Gore-Tex membrane?
113705.e: PTFE is also the non-stick coating on many frying pans. The material is very smooth and resists chemicals.
113705.m: PTFE also coats many frying pans.

113706.q: According to the manufacturer, roughly how many times smaller than a drop of water are the pores of the membrane?
113706.e: According to the manufacturer, the pores are about 20,000 times smaller than a drop of water. So one square centimetre contains an unimaginable number of pores.
113706.m: The pores of the membrane are tiny compared with a drop.

113707.q: Why is the plastic of the Gore-Tex membrane controversial?
a: Similar substances hardly break down in nature
113707.e: PTFE belongs to a group of chemicals, PFAS for short, that stay in the environment for a very long time. That is why people are looking for alternatives.
113707.m: Some plastics stay in the environment for a very long time.

113708.q: What does “breathable” mean for a rain jacket?
a: Sweat can get out as vapour
You can breathe in it under water
113708.e: A breathable jacket lets water vapour from the body out. This means you do not get wet inside from sweating.
113708.m: Breathable means vapour can get out.

113709.q: What percentage of the volume of a typical aerogel is air?
113709.e: Typical aerogels are made up of 90 to 99.8 per cent pores full of air. That is why they are among the lightest solid materials of all.
113709.m: An aerogel is almost all air.

113710.q: What nickname does aerogel have because of how it looks?
113710.e: Aerogel looks bluish, see-through and misty. That is why it is also called “frozen smoke”.

113711.q: How is an aerogel made from a gel?
a: The liquid in the gel is replaced by gas
113711.e: In 1931, Samuel Kistler was the first to replace the liquid in a gel with gas. What was left was a fine, solid framework full of air.
113711.m: In an aerogel, the liquid of a gel has been replaced by gas.

113712.q: What is aerogel especially suitable for as a building material?
113712.e: Heat can hardly spread in the tiny pores. That is why aerogel insulates extremely well, but it is mechanically delicate.
113712.m: Aerogel is an excellent heat insulator.

113713.q: What did NASA's Stardust probe collect using aerogel?
113713.e: Stardust flew past the comet Wild 2 and caught dust particles in aerogel. The particles were gently slowed down in it and brought back to Earth in 2006.
113713.m: Stardust caught comet dust with aerogel.

113714.q: What is the most common aerogel made of?
a: The same substance as sand and glass
113714.e: The best-known aerogel is made of silicon dioxide. This substance is also found in quartz sand and glass.
113714.m: The most common aerogel is made of the substance in sand and glass.

113715.q: Why can a gel for aerogel not simply be left to dry in the air?
113715.e: With normal drying, the remaining liquid pulls the tiny pores together. So a special drying method is needed to keep the framework intact.
113715.m: Aerogel needs a special drying method.

113716.q: Which aerogel product for buildings did Empa develop with an industry partner?
a: An insulating plaster for outside walls
113716.e: Empa developed a plaster with aerogel that insulates much better than ordinary plaster. It is especially suitable for renovating old houses.
113716.m: Aerogel plaster insulates old outside walls especially well.

113717.q: What happens to a bent shape-memory alloy when you heat it?
a: It goes back to its original shape
113717.e: Shape-memory alloys “remember” a shape given to them earlier. When heated, they return to this shape.
113717.m: Shape-memory alloys return to their shape when heated.

113718.q: Which two metals make up the best-known shape-memory alloy, Nitinol?
113718.e: Nitinol consists of roughly equal parts of nickel and titanium. The letters NiTi in the name stand for these two metals.
113718.m: Nitinol is made of nickel and titanium.

113719.q: What is an alloy such as Nitinol?
a: A plastic made from crude oil
113719.e: An alloy is made when metals are melted together. Nitinol is made of nickel and titanium.
113719.m: An alloy is a mixture of metals.

113720.q: Which medical tubes made of Nitinol keep narrowed blood vessels open?
113720.e: A stent is put in folded up and opens out inside the body. Nitinol is suitable because it moves back into its shape at body temperature.
113720.m: Nitinol stents keep blood vessels open.

113721.q: In which area of dentistry are Nitinol wires used?
113721.e: Nitinol wires in braces apply a gentle, even force for a long time. This slowly moves the teeth.

113722.q: What is the property called that lets Nitinol bend a lot at room temperature and spring back by itself?
113722.e: Superelastic Nitinol can be bent much further than normal steel and springs back afterwards. This is used for parts that should not stay bent.
113722.m: Superelastic metal springs back after being bent a lot.

113723.q: What changes in a shape-memory alloy when it gets warm?
a: The arrangement of the atoms in the crystal
113723.e: When heated, the atoms arrange themselves in a different crystal pattern. This makes the metal return to its old shape.
113723.m: The shape-memory effect is based on a new arrangement of the atoms.

113724.q: Which everyday objects are made from superelastic shape-memory alloys so that they do not bend out of shape?
113724.e: Glasses frames made of Nitinol can be twisted a lot and still return to their shape. This makes them very tough.
113724.m: Nitinol glasses survive being bent a lot.

113725.q: What raw material is traditional ceramics mainly made from?
113725.e: Clay is easy to shape when it is damp. After drying and firing, it becomes ceramic.
113725.m: Traditional ceramics are made of clay.

113726.q: What makes shaped clay permanently hard?
113726.e: When it is fired at several hundred to over a thousand degrees, the minerals in the clay change. Afterwards the piece is hard and no longer softens in water.

113727.q: In which country was porcelain invented?
113727.e: Porcelain was invented in China and for a long time was a valuable trade good. That is why porcelain is also called “china” in English.

113728.q: How can you easily recognise porcelain?
a: It is white and thin, almost see-through
113728.e: Porcelain is made from a white clay called kaolin and fired at a very high temperature. Thin pieces even let some light through.

113729.q: Why was porcelain once called “white gold” in Europe?
a: Because only kings were allowed to make it
113729.e: For a long time, only China could make porcelain, and it was very expensive in Europe. The first European factory was not founded until 1710, in Meissen.
113729.m: Porcelain was once as valuable as gold.

113730.q: What were most of the heat-shield tiles of the Space Shuttle made of?
113730.e: The tiles were made of ceramic fibres. They protected the spacecraft during re-entry from temperatures far above 1000 degrees.
113730.m: Ceramics protect spacecraft from great heat.

113731.q: Which property is typical of ceramics?
113731.e: Ceramics are very hard and resist heat. But they break easily if dropped because they can hardly change shape.

113732.q: What is the glassy layer put on ceramics called?
113732.e: The glaze melts into a smooth layer during firing. It makes the vessel watertight and often colourful too.
113732.m: A glaze makes ceramics smooth and watertight.

113733.q: Which building material belongs to ceramics?
113733.e: Bricks are shaped from clay or loam and fired. That makes them building ceramics.

113734.q: Which raw material is the main ingredient of ordinary glass?
113734.e: Ordinary glass is made mostly of quartz sand, which is silicon dioxide. Other additives are added too.
113734.m: Glass is made mainly from quartz sand.

113735.q: What happens to glass when you heat it strongly?
a: It becomes soft and can be shaped
It becomes as hard as stone
113735.e: When heated, glass slowly becomes soft and runny. That is why glassblowers can shape it.

113736.q: Which rock is a natural volcanic glass?
113736.e: Obsidian forms when lava cools so quickly that no crystals form. In the Stone Age, people made sharp blades from it.
113736.m: Obsidian is natural glass from volcanoes.

113737.q: Why does window glass let light through?
a: It is as thin as paper
113737.e: Glass lets visible light pass through almost freely. That is why it is suitable for windows.

113738.q: In the laminated safety glass of a car windscreen, what is between the two panes of glass?
113738.e: The plastic film holds the splinters in place if the windscreen breaks. This means nobody is hurt by sharp pieces of glass.
113738.m: In laminated safety glass, a film holds the splinters in place.

113739.q: At roughly what temperature is glass melted from its raw materials?
113739.e: The raw materials are melted in tank furnaces at roughly 1400 to 1600 degrees. This takes a lot of energy.
113739.m: Glass only melts at very high temperatures.

113740.q: What is carried through fibre-optic cables?
113740.e: In glass fibres, data is passed along as light signals. This is how fast internet reaches people's homes.
113740.m: Fibre-optic cables carry data with light.

113741.q: Why is soda added to quartz sand when making glass?
113741.e: Pure quartz only melts at over 1700 degrees. Soda acts as a flux and lowers the melting temperature a lot.
113741.m: Soda makes glass easier to melt.

113742.q: What is the tool called that glassblowers use to blow liquid glass into vessels?
113742.e: The blowpipe is a long metal tube. The glassblower uses it to pick up a lump of glass and blow it up.
113742.m: Glassblowers shape glass with a blowpipe.

113743.q: In Switzerland, what goes into the PET collection?
113743.e: Only drinks bottles go into the PET collection. Other plastics get in the way of recycling.
113743.m: Only drinks bottles go into the PET collection.

113744.q: What does the recycling symbol with a number on plastic packaging show?
113744.e: The code with the numbers 1 to 7 shows which plastic the packaging is made of. The number 1, for example, stands for PET.
113744.m: The number in the recycling symbol tells you the type of plastic.

113745.q: How many PET drinks bottles are collected and recycled in Switzerland?
113745.e: In Switzerland, more than three quarters of PET drinks bottles are collected and recycled. That is high compared with other countries.
113745.m: In Switzerland, most PET bottles are collected.

113746.q: What happens when plastic waste is used for energy recovery?
a: It is burned and the energy is used
It is melted into new bottles
It is buried in the ground
It is piped into the sea
113746.e: Plastic is burned in the waste incineration plant. The heat is used for electricity and district heating, but the material itself is lost.
113746.m: In energy recovery, waste is burned to produce energy.

113747.q: What do you call recycling in which the material becomes a product of lower quality?
113747.e: If, for example, a bottle is turned into a park bench, the material can hardly be used for anything high-quality later on. This is called downcycling.
113747.m: Downcycling turns material into a product of lower quality.

113748.q: Which item of clothing is often made from recycled PET bottles?
113748.e: Polyester fibres can be spun from PET bottles. They are used to make fleece jumpers, for example.
113748.m: Old PET bottles can be made into fleece.

113749.q: What are the small pieces called that PET bottles are chopped into during recycling?
113749.e: The bottles are sorted, chopped up and washed. The clean flakes are then melted down and processed further.
113749.m: During recycling, PET bottles are chopped into flakes.

113750.q: What happens in the chemical recycling of plastics?
a: They are broken down into their basic building blocks
113750.e: In chemical recycling, the long chains of molecules are split into smaller building blocks. These can be used to make new plastics again.
113750.m: Chemical recycling breaks plastics down into their building blocks.

113751.q: Which technology do modern sorting plants use to recognise the type of plastic automatically?
113751.e: Each type of plastic reflects near-infrared light in a typical way. Sensors recognise this, and air jets blow the pieces into the right container.
113751.m: Sorting plants recognise plastics with near-infrared light.

113752.q: Which process in nature is the model for self-healing materials?
113752.e: When we cut ourselves, the body closes the wound by itself. Researchers want materials to repair small damage by themselves too.

113753.q: What happens when a crack forms in a plastic with built-in microcapsules?
a: The capsules burst and fill the crack
The capsules pull the crack apart
113753.e: The crack breaks open the tiny capsules. A liquid healing agent flows out, fills the crack and hardens.
113753.m: Microcapsules release a healing agent when there is a crack.

113754.q: Which substance do bacteria in self-healing concrete make to close cracks?
113754.e: The bacteria produce calcium carbonate, which is limestone. It builds up in the crack and seals it.
113754.m: Bacteria in concrete seal cracks with limestone.

113755.q: What makes the sleeping bacteria in self-healing concrete become active?
113755.e: The bacterial spores rest in the concrete until water reaches them through a crack. Then they become active and start working.
113755.m: Only water getting in wakes up the bacteria in the concrete.

113756.q: In 2023, researchers found that lumps of lime can seal cracks by themselves in the concrete of which ancient culture?
113756.e: Roman concrete contains small lumps of lime. If water gets into a crack, lime dissolves and fills the crack again.
113756.m: Roman concrete can seal small cracks by itself.

113757.q: What is the main advantage of self-healing materials?
a: They last longer and need fewer repairs
They are always cheaper than other materials
113757.e: Small damage is repaired before it gets bigger. This makes parts last longer, and less material and work are needed.
113757.m: Self-healing materials make parts last longer.

113758.q: Which product already has self-healing coatings against small scratches?
113758.e: There are clear coats in which fine scratches disappear again with heat. They are used on cars, for example.
113758.m: Some car paints heal fine scratches by themselves.

113759.q: How can healing be triggered in some self-healing plastics?
113759.e: In certain plastics, broken chemical bonds can form again when heated. This closes up the damage.
113759.m: Heat can make some plastics heal.

113760.q: In which municipality is Empa's NEST research building?
113760.e: NEST stands on the Empa site in Dübendorf in the canton of Zurich. Research into new building and energy technologies is carried out there.

113761.q: What is tested in Empa's NEST research building in Dübendorf?
113761.e: In NEST, researchers try out new building materials and energy technologies under real conditions. What works well can later be used in normal houses.
113761.m: New building technologies are tested in NEST.

113762.q: What is special about the way NEST is built?
a: Research modules can be fitted and replaced again
The building turns with the sun
The building is made entirely of glass
113762.e: The individual modules, called units, are fitted into a fixed basic framework. When a project is finished, it can be replaced by a new one.
113762.m: In NEST, research modules can be swapped.

113763.q: Why do real people live and work in the NEST research building?
a: So that new technologies are tested in everyday life
Because the building is a normal hotel
Because a hospital is based there
Because otherwise the building would collapse
113763.e: NEST has flats and offices. This shows whether new technologies also work in daily use and whether people like them.
113763.m: In NEST, technologies are tested in real everyday life.

113764.q: What is the aim of the “Urban Mining and Recycling” unit in NEST?
a: All building materials should be reusable
The building should be as heavy as possible
113764.e: The unit is built so that all the materials can be separated again and reused. In this way, the building serves as a store of materials.
113764.m: Buildings can act as stores of reusable materials.

113765.q: What was the focus of the “DFAB House” unit in NEST?
a: Digital building with robots and 3D printing
Building by hand with clay only
113765.e: For the DFAB House, ETH Zurich worked with digitally controlled robots and 3D printing. Many parts were made directly from computer data.
113765.m: Digital building was tried out in the DFAB House.

113766.q: The HiLo research unit in NEST has a thin, curved concrete roof. Why does this shape save material?
a: A vault can carry a lot with little material
A curved roof needs no walls
Snow never lies on a curved roof
113766.e: A vault carries the load out to the sides like a bridge. That is why it can be much thinner than a flat roof.
113766.m: A curved roof can carry a lot with little material.

113767.q: What is the fixed basic framework of the NEST research building for?
a: It carries the replaceable research modules
It is used as a car park
113767.e: The basic framework contains stairs, pipes and cables, and platforms. The individual research modules are docked onto it and later swapped.
113767.m: NEST's basic framework carries the research modules.

113768.q: How did Hermann Ebbinghaus test how quickly we forget what we have learnt?
a: He learnt meaningless syllables by heart himself
He watched rats in the laboratory
He took pictures of the brain
113768.e: In experiments on himself, Hermann Ebbinghaus learnt meaningless syllables and checked how much he still knew later. This led to the forgetting curve.
113768.m: Ebbinghaus studied how quickly we forget.

113769.q: What does the forgetting curve show?
a: You forget the most shortly after learning
You forget the same amount every day
You only forget after a year
What you learn is never forgotten
113769.e: Right after learning, how much you remember drops steeply, and later only slowly. That is why it pays to revise early.
113769.m: Without revision, you forget most things soon after learning them.

113770.q: According to research, which learning strategy is usually more effective?
a: Revising the material spread over several days
Learning everything in one long night before the test
Reading it once and never revising
Only learning on the day of the test
113770.e: Spread-out learning with breaks leads to better remembering than cramming everything at once. Experts call this the spacing effect.
113770.m: If you spread out your revision, you remember more.

113771.q: What did the famous Bobo doll experiment show?
a: Children copy what adults show them
Children forget what they see at once
113771.e: Children watched a film in which an adult hit a doll. Afterwards, many of the children copied this behaviour. The psychologist Albert Bandura called this learning from a model.
113771.m: Children learn a lot by copying role models.

113772.q: A dog gets a treat every time it sits down. Soon it sits down much more often. How has it learnt this?
113772.e: A behaviour becomes more frequent when it is rewarded and less frequent when it is punished. Experts call this operant conditioning.
113772.m: Rewarded behaviour is shown more often.

113773.q: What did animals learn in the so-called Skinner box?
a: To press a lever to get food
To recognise themselves in a mirror
113773.e: In the Skinner box, rats or pigeons learnt to press a lever or peck a key to get food. This allowed Burrhus F. Skinner to measure learning precisely.
113773.m: In the Skinner box, animals learnt through food rewards.

113774.q: What does learning by trial and error mean?
a: You keep trying things until something works
You read the whole instructions first
113774.e: When learning by trial and error, you try out different ways. You keep what works, and with every attempt you get faster.
113774.m: Through trial and error, you get faster over time.

113775.q: According to research on learning, what helps more than just reading something through several times?
a: Copying out the text in colour
Listening to loud music at the same time
113775.e: When you test yourself, you have to actively bring the knowledge back from memory. This strengthens the memory more than reading passively.
113775.m: Testing yourself makes learning last longer.

113776.q: Whom did the greylag goslings follow that Konrad Lorenz saw first after hatching?
113776.e: Young geese follow the first moving creature they see shortly after hatching. Lorenz called this kind of learning imprinting.
113776.m: In imprinting, young animals learn within a short time whom to follow.

113777.q: What do you call a stimulus that causes a reaction without any learning?
113777.e: A puff of air into the eye, for example, makes you blink without any learning. Stimuli like this are called unconditioned stimuli.
113777.m: An unconditioned stimulus works without any previous learning.

113778.q: What is it called when a learnt reaction disappears because the stimulus keeps occurring for a long time without the reward?
113778.e: If nothing follows the learnt stimulus again and again, the reaction becomes weaker. Experts call this extinction.
113778.m: Without the link, a learnt reaction becomes weaker.

113779.q: A dog has unlearnt drooling at the sound of a bell. What can still happen after a longer break?
a: It suddenly drools briefly at the sound again
It becomes afraid of the bell
It no longer hears the bell
113779.e: A reaction that has been unlearnt is not completely forgotten. After a break, it can briefly come back. Experts call this spontaneous recovery.
113779.m: Unlearnt reactions can come back after a break.

113780.q: In an experiment in 1920, which animal did “Little Albert” learn to be afraid of?
113780.e: Every time the toddler saw the rat, a loud bang was made. Soon he was afraid of the rat on its own. Today the experiment is seen as unethical.
113780.m: Fear can also be learnt through conditioning.

113781.q: A child has learnt to be afraid of one particular dog. What often happens?
a: It is also afraid of similar dogs
It is only afraid of that one dog
It suddenly likes all dogs especially
It is now only afraid of cats
113781.e: A learnt fear often spreads to similar stimuli. This is called stimulus generalisation.
113781.m: Similar stimuli can set off the same learnt reaction.

113782.q: A dog only gets food after a high note, never after a low note. How does it react after a while?
a: It only drools at the high note
It drools equally at both notes
It no longer drools at either note
It only drools at the low note
113782.e: The dog learns to tell similar notes apart. Only the note that is followed by food sets off the reaction.
113782.m: Animals can learn to tell similar stimuli apart.

113783.q: What did the researcher John B. Watson want to show with experiments such as “Little Albert”?
a: That feelings such as fear can be learnt
That fear is inborn and cannot be changed
113783.e: Watson showed that fear can also be learnt through conditioning. He mainly studied behaviour that can be observed.
113783.m: Feelings such as fear can also be learnt.

113784.q: After an upset stomach, you feel disgusted for a long time by the food you ate beforehand. What is this learnt effect called?
113784.e: Even a single link between food and feeling sick can create a strong dislike. This is a special form of classical conditioning.
113784.m: A taste aversion can develop after just one bad experience.

113785.q: Which country did the researcher Ivan Pavlov come from?
113785.e: Ivan Petrovich Pavlov was a Russian physiologist. He lived from 1849 to 1936.
113785.m: Ivan Pavlov was a Russian researcher.

113786.q: What did Pavlov receive the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for in 1904?
a: For discovering the circulation of the blood
113786.e: Pavlov received the Nobel Prize for his work on the digestive glands. His famous learning experiments only grew out of this research.
113786.m: Pavlov received the Nobel Prize for research on digestion.

113787.q: Which bodily reaction of the dogs did Pavlov measure in his experiments?
113787.e: Pavlov collected and measured the liquid from the dogs' salivary glands. This let him find out exactly when and how strongly they reacted.
113787.m: Pavlov measured the flow of saliva in his dogs.

113788.q: With which animals did Ivan Pavlov carry out his famous learning experiments?
113788.e: Pavlov did research with dogs in St Petersburg for decades. He showed that they learn to link a signal with food.
113788.m: Pavlov did his learning experiments with dogs.

113789.q: In stories about Pavlov's experiment, which stimulus is usually linked with the food?
113789.e: In many accounts, a bell rings before the food. Pavlov himself also used a metronome and buzzers, among other things.
113789.m: With Pavlov's dog, a sound announces the food.

113790.q: What did Pavlov call the learnt reaction of his dogs?
113790.e: A conditioned reflex only develops through experience. Inborn reflexes such as blinking, on the other hand, do not need to be learnt.
113790.m: A conditioned reflex develops through experience.

113791.q: What do people mean when they say someone reacts “like Pavlov's dog”?
a: They react automatically to a learnt signal
113791.e: The expression describes a reaction that follows a familiar signal without thinking. One example is reaching for your mobile phone when it rings.

113792.q: When must the sound be heard so that the dog learns the link to the food best?
a: Long after the food has been eaten
113792.e: The signal has to announce the food, so it must come just before it. Then the dog learns fastest that the two belong together.
113792.m: A signal is learnt best when it comes shortly before the event.

113793.q: What is motivation called that comes from enjoying the activity itself?
113793.e: If you do something because it is fun or interesting, you are intrinsically motivated. The motivation comes from inside.

113794.q: A child only learns in order to get a reward. What is this kind of motivation called?
113794.e: With this motivation, the incentive comes from outside, for example through marks, praise or money. The activity itself is not the main thing.

113795.q: Which needs form the bottom level of Maslow's hierarchy of needs?
a: Basic physical needs such as food and sleep
113795.e: First, hunger, thirst and the need for sleep must be satisfied. According to this theory, only then do higher needs become important.
113795.m: At the bottom of the hierarchy of needs are the basic physical needs.

113798.q: What is the state called in which you are completely absorbed in an activity and forget the time?
113798.e: The psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi described flow. It often happens when a task is neither too easy nor too hard.
113798.m: In flow, you are completely absorbed in an activity.

113799.q: What can happen if you are regularly rewarded for an activity that you enjoy doing anyway?
a: Your enjoyment of the activity can drop
You immediately get better at it
You no longer need any sleep
113799.e: Experiments show that rewards can push aside your own desire to do something. Experts call this the overjustification effect.
113799.m: Rewards can reduce the enjoyment of something.

113800.q: According to goal-setting theory, which goals boost performance the most?
a: Vague goals such as “Do your best”
113800.e: Edwin Locke and Gary Latham found that clear, demanding goals lead to better performance than unclear ones. It is important that you accept the goal.
113800.m: Clear and demanding goals spur you on.

113801.q: How many basic emotions did Paul Ekman originally name?
113801.e: Ekman named joy, sadness, fear and anger, among others. These basic feelings show in typical facial expressions.
113801.m: Ekman originally described six basic feelings.

113802.q: What does the amygdala in the brain do?
a: It raises the alarm when there is danger
113802.e: The amygdala judges in a flash whether something is dangerous. It can trigger a fear reaction even before we think.
113802.m: The amygdala raises the alarm when there is danger.

113803.q: Which naturalist wrote a book in 1872 about the expression of the emotions in humans and animals?
113803.e: Darwin compared the facial expressions of humans and animals. He thought that many ways of expressing feelings are inborn.
113803.m: Darwin also studied how feelings become visible.

113804.q: What did Paul Ekman's research in Papua New Guinea show?
a: Basic feelings are shown in similar ways on faces all over the world
Every people has completely different facial expressions
113804.e: Ekman showed photos of faces to people who had no contact with Western media. They recognised the basic feelings in a similar way to people in other countries.
113804.m: Basic feelings are recognised in similar ways in all cultures.

113805.q: Which system in the brain do areas that are strongly involved in feelings belong to?
113805.e: The limbic system lies deep in the brain. It processes feelings and is closely linked with memory.

113806.q: How did the psychologist Robert Plutchik arrange the emotions in his “wheel of emotions”?
a: Similar ones next to each other, opposites facing each other
By how loudly they are expressed
113806.e: Robert Plutchik arranged eight basic emotions in a circle. Joy, for example, is opposite sadness.
113806.m: Plutchik arranged emotions in a wheel.

113807.q: What is the ability to recognise your own and other people's feelings and handle them well called?
113807.e: The term became very well known in the 1990s through Daniel Goleman. It includes self-awareness and empathy.
113807.m: Emotional intelligence helps you deal with feelings.

113808.q: Which feeling is one of Ekman's basic emotions?
113808.e: All over the world, disgust shows in a typical wrinkling of the nose. Feelings such as jealousy or pride are seen as more complex.
113808.m: Disgust is a basic feeling with a typical facial expression.

113809.q: In a famous experiment, people had to say which line was the same length as another. The others in the group deliberately gave wrong answers. What did many of the test subjects do?
a: They gave the wrong answer too
They left the room at once
They did not notice the wrong answers
They could not see the lines
113809.e: Even though the task was very easy, many went along with the wrong majority. In this way, the psychologist Solomon Asch showed how strong group pressure is.
113809.m: Many people go along with a majority, even when it is wrong.

a: You take part in a dare because all your friends are doing it
You eat because you are hungry
You sleep because you are tired
You put on a jacket because it is cold
113810.e: With group pressure, you do something not because you want to, but because you want to belong.
113810.m: Group pressure means doing something only because the others are doing it.

113811.q: What helps you resist group pressure?
a: Saying no clearly and sticking to your own opinion
Always doing what the majority wants
113811.e: If you know what you want and say so calmly, you are less easily influenced. It also helps to have a friend who thinks the same way.
113811.m: If you stick to your opinion, you resist group pressure better.

113812.q: What do you call it when someone adapts their opinion or behaviour to a group?
113812.e: Conformity means adapting to the norms or opinions of a group. Group pressure can make it stronger.
113812.m: Conformity is adapting to a group.

113813.q: In the Asch experiment, what happened when one other person in the group also gave the right answer?
a: Going along with the majority dropped sharply
The experiment had to be stopped
Going along with the majority rose sharply
113813.e: Just one ally made it much easier to disagree with the majority. People no longer felt alone.
113813.m: A single ally helps you resist group pressure.

113814.q: What is the term for pressure from people of your own age?
113814.e: “Peers” are people of the same age, such as friends or classmates. Their influence is especially strong in the teenage years.
113814.m: Peer pressure is pressure from people your own age.

113815.q: What do you call it when a group makes bad decisions because it wants to agree?
113815.e: Irving Janis described groupthink. Critical opinions are held back so that harmony is kept.
113815.m: In groupthink, critical voices are held back.

113816.q: What is the effect called where people are less likely to help in an emergency when many others are watching?
113816.e: Everyone thinks that someone else will help. So nobody feels responsible.
113816.m: With the bystander effect, everyone relies on the others.

113817.q: What do you call a simplified, generalised idea about a whole group of people?
113817.e: A stereotype gives all members of a group the same characteristics. This is not fair to the individual people.
113817.m: A stereotype generalises about a whole group.

113819.q: According to the contact hypothesis, what can reduce prejudice between groups?
a: Positive contact on an equal footing
113819.e: When people from different groups meet as equals and work together, prejudice often decreases. This idea goes back to Gordon Allport.
113819.m: Meeting as equals breaks down prejudice.

113820.q: A teacher divided her class by eye colour and favoured one group. What did the children learn from this?
a: How to work out eye colour
That brown eyes make you cleverer
113820.e: The American teacher Jane Elliott did this exercise in 1968. The children experienced for themselves how it feels to be treated badly because of a random feature.
113820.m: A random feature can lead to discrimination.

113821.q: What is the tendency called to pay attention mainly to information that confirms your own opinion?
113821.e: With confirmation bias, we mainly notice what fits our opinion and overlook examples that go against it. This can make prejudices stick.
113821.m: Confirmation bias makes us see mainly information that fits.

113822.q: In Muzafer Sherif's summer camp experiment, what reduced the hostility between two groups?
113822.e: The young people had to solve tasks that could only be managed together. After that, quarrelling and putting each other down decreased.

113823.q: What do you call the tendency to favour your own group over other groups?
113823.e: Even when people are put into groups at random, they often favour their own. This can strengthen prejudice against others.
113823.m: People often favour their own group.

113824.q: Apart from a vase, what can you see in the ambiguous picture known as the “Rubin vase”?
113824.e: The white area in the middle is a vase, and the dark edges on the left and right are two faces looking at each other. Depending on how you look, you see one or the other.
113824.m: The Rubin vase shows a vase or two faces.

113825.q: What is special about an ambiguous picture?
a: You can see it in two ways
You can only see it in the dark
113825.e: With an ambiguous picture, your perception jumps back and forth between two interpretations. But you cannot see both pictures at the same time.
113825.m: An ambiguous picture can be seen in two ways.

113826.q: What is confusing about the Necker cube, a cube drawn with lines?
a: You cannot tell which side is at the front
It disappears when you look at it
113826.e: The Geneva researcher Louis Albert Necker described this cube in 1832. The view jumps back and forth: sometimes one face is at the front, sometimes the other.
113826.m: With the Necker cube, the front side jumps back and forth.

113827.q: Which two animals are shown in the well-known ambiguous picture described by Joseph Jastrow in 1899?
113827.e: Depending on how you look, you see a duck's head with a beak or a rabbit's head with ears. The philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein later made the picture even more famous.
113827.m: Jastrow's ambiguous picture hides a duck or a rabbit.

113828.q: Which two figures are shown in the ambiguous picture “My Wife and My Mother-in-Law”?
a: A young woman and an old woman
113828.e: What is the ear and chin of the young woman becomes the eye and nose of the old woman. Many people at first see only one of the two.
113828.m: The same picture can show a young or an old woman.

113829.q: What do you experience when you look at an ambiguous picture?
a: You see both interpretations in turn, but never at the same time
You always see both interpretations at the same time
The picture really changes its colours
The picture moves on the paper
113829.e: The brain chooses one interpretation at a time. At that moment the other one cannot be seen, even if you know it is there.
113829.m: With an ambiguous picture, the brain switches between two interpretations.

113830.q: Which distinction in perception does the Rubin vase use?
113830.e: The brain splits a picture into a figure in the foreground and a background. In the Rubin vase, both parts can be the figure.

113831.q: How can you see the Schröder staircase?
a: Once from above and once from below
113831.e: You can see the drawn staircase as a normal staircase from above or as an upside-down staircase from below. The view suddenly flips.
113831.m: The Schröder staircase flips between two views.

113832.q: What does the abbreviation REM in REM sleep stand for?
113832.e: In REM sleep, the eyes move quickly back and forth under the eyelids. That is where the name comes from.
113832.m: In REM sleep, the eyes move quickly.

113833.q: What did researchers observe in sleeping people in the 1950s?
a: That the brain switches off completely
113833.e: In 1953 in Chicago, Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman discovered REM sleep with its rapid eye movements. This was the start of modern sleep research.
113833.m: REM sleep was discovered in the 1950s.

113834.q: In which phase of sleep do people have especially vivid dreams?
113834.e: People woken from REM sleep especially often report vivid dreams. But people also dream in other phases.
113834.m: Vivid dreams happen mainly in REM sleep.

113835.q: Roughly how long does a sleep cycle last in an adult?
113835.e: A cycle of light sleep, deep sleep and REM sleep lasts about an hour and a half. You go through several of them each night.
113835.m: A sleep cycle lasts about an hour and a half.

113836.q: Which method is used in a sleep laboratory to measure brain waves?
113836.e: In electroencephalography, or EEG for short, electrodes are stuck onto the scalp. They record the electrical activity of the brain.
113836.m: Brain waves are measured with an EEG.

113837.q: Which hormone makes us tired in the evening and is produced in larger amounts in the dark?
113837.e: Melatonin is made in the pineal gland, mainly in the dark. Bright light in the evening can slow down its production.
113837.m: Melatonin is the hormone that makes you tired.

113838.q: How many hours of sleep a night do expert bodies recommend for teenagers aged 13 to 18?
113838.e: Teenagers need a lot of sleep because their bodies and brains are still developing. Expert bodies recommend 8 to 10 hours.
113838.m: Teenagers need about eight to ten hours of sleep.

113839.q: The Zurich researcher Alexander Borbély explained sleep with two processes. What are they?
a: Sleep pressure and the body clock
113839.e: The longer you are awake, the greater the sleep pressure. The body clock also decides when we get tired. The model from 1982 is still used today.
113839.m: Sleep pressure and the body clock control sleep together.

113840.q: What does the word “circadian” in circadian rhythm mean?
113840.e: The word comes from the Latin “circa diem”, meaning “about a day”. The body clock runs on a roughly 24-hour cycle.
113840.m: The body clock follows a rhythm of about one day.

113841.q: What do you call positive, motivating stress?
113841.e: Eustress motivates you and helps you perform, for example before a competition. Stress that weighs you down, on the other hand, is called distress.

113842.q: Which organs release stress hormones such as cortisol and adrenaline?
113842.e: The adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys. Under strain, they release hormones into the blood that put the body on alert.
113842.m: The adrenal glands make stress hormones.

113843.q: What is the body's quick emergency response to a threat called?
113843.e: Walter Cannon described how the body prepares in a flash to fight or run away. This response already helped our ancestors to survive.
113843.m: In danger, the body prepares to fight or run away.

113844.q: What happens in the body during acute stress?
113844.e: During stress, the heart pumps faster to supply the muscles with blood. Digestion, on the other hand, is slowed down.
113844.m: During stress, the heart beats faster.

113845.q: At what level of tension does a test usually go best?
a: At a medium level of tension
Only when you are very tired
113845.e: A bit of tension makes you alert and focused, but too much blocks you. Experts call this link the Yerkes-Dodson law.
113845.m: A medium level of tension usually leads to the best performance.

113847.q: Which measure has been shown to help reduce stress?
a: Always being on your mobile phone
113847.e: Sport and exercise help to break down stress hormones and improve your mood. Getting enough sleep and taking breaks are also important.

113848.q: What can happen if stress lasts for a very long time?
a: The heart beats slower and slower
113848.e: With constant stress, the body's strength is used up at some point. The researcher Hans Selye called this the exhaustion stage.
113848.m: Constant stress can lead to exhaustion.

113849.q: Which country did the child researcher Jean Piaget come from?
113849.e: Jean Piaget was born in Neuchâtel in 1896 and did research in Geneva for a long time. He became one of the best-known developmental psychologists in the world.
113849.m: Jean Piaget was a Swiss researcher.

113853.q: A child thinks there is more water in a tall, narrow glass than there was before in the wide glass. What has the child not yet understood?
113853.e: The amount of water stays the same, even if it looks different. But younger children are fooled by the height of the water.
113853.m: An amount stays the same, even if its shape changes.

113854.q: According to Piaget, what can young people do in the formal operational stage, from about 11 or 12 years old?
a: Grasp things for the first time
Speak words for the first time
Recognise objects for the first time
113854.e: In this stage, you can think about thoughts, make hypotheses and test them logically. You no longer depend on things you can see and touch.
113854.m: Young people learn to think abstractly.

113855.q: What did Jean Piaget mainly study?
113855.e: Piaget watched children closely and gave them small tasks. That is how he found out how their thinking develops step by step.
113855.m: Piaget studied how children learn to think.

113856.q: What did Piaget's three mountains experiment show in younger children?
a: They find it hard to see things from someone else's point of view
113856.e: The children had to say how a doll would see the mountain landscape from another side. Younger children usually described their own view. Piaget called this egocentrism.
113856.m: Younger children often start from their own point of view.

113857.q: What did Piaget already study scientifically as a teenager?
113857.e: As a teenager, Piaget was already publishing articles about snails and other molluscs. Later he earned a doctorate in natural sciences.
113857.m: Piaget started out as a young naturalist.

113858.q: Which three parts make up the so-called habit loop?
113858.e: A cue starts a well-practised behaviour, which is followed by a reward. Through repetition, this loop becomes more and more automatic.
113858.m: Habits form from a cue, a routine and a reward.

113859.q: In a study by Phillippa Lally in 2009, how long did it take on average for a new behaviour to become a habit?
113859.e: On average it took about two months, but there were big differences depending on the person and the behaviour. Some needed much less time, others much longer.
113859.m: A new habit often takes about two months.

113860.e: Well-practised routines are stored deep in the brain. This means habits can run almost without thinking.
113860.m: Habits are stored in the brain.

113861.q: You often hear that a new habit forms in exactly 21 days. Is that true?
a: No, it is an inaccurate rule of thumb
113861.e: The 21-day rule is not backed up by science. How long it takes depends on the person and the behaviour.
113861.m: The 21-day rule for habits is not scientifically proven.

113862.q: Why do you stop hearing the ticking of a clock after a while?
a: The brain filters out sounds that stay the same
113862.e: The brain mainly pays attention to new things. Over time, it filters out a harmless stimulus that stays the same.
113862.m: Harmless stimuli that stay the same are filtered out over time.

113863.q: Which plan helps most to really practise every day?
a: “When I get home from school, I will practise for ten minutes.”
“I will practise when I feel like it.”
113863.e: An if-then plan links the new behaviour to a fixed situation. This makes you less likely to forget it.
113863.m: If-then plans help you stick to your intentions.

113864.q: Why do habits take the load off the brain?
a: They need a lot of concentration
They have to be learnt again every time
113864.e: When you brush your teeth or ride a bike, you do not have to think about every step. This leaves attention free for new things.

113865.q: Which strategy often helps you get rid of an unwanted habit?
a: Changing the cue in your surroundings
113865.e: If, for example, you put your mobile phone in another room while studying, you come across the cue less often. This makes it easier to drop the old behaviour.
113865.m: If you remove the cue, it is easier to break a habit.

a: Natural substances from plants that are often poisonous
113866.e: Alkaloids are made mainly by plants. Many have a strong effect on the body, for example caffeine or nicotine.
113866.m: Alkaloids are strong, often poisonous plant substances.

113867.q: Which poisonous alkaloid forms in green patches on potatoes?
113867.e: Green patches and sprouts on potatoes contain solanine. That is why you cut them away generously before cooking.
113867.m: Green patches on potatoes contain poisonous solanine.

113868.q: Which well-known alkaloid is found in coffee beans?
113868.e: Caffeine is an alkaloid that keeps you awake. It is also found in tea leaves, for example.
113868.m: The caffeine in coffee is also an alkaloid.

113869.q: Which alkaloid comes from the tobacco plant?
113869.e: The tobacco plant makes nicotine in its leaves. For insects it is a strong poison.
113869.m: Nicotine is the poisonous alkaloid of the tobacco plant.

113870.q: What do most alkaloids taste like?
113870.e: Most alkaloids taste bitter. The bitter taste often warns animals and people of something poisonous.
113870.m: Many plant poisons taste bitter and so warn of danger.

113871.q: What are alkaloids probably for in the plant itself?
a: Protection from animals that eat them
113871.e: Plants cannot run away. Poisonous and bitter substances such as alkaloids stop many animals from eating them.
113871.m: Plants protect themselves with alkaloids from animals that want to eat them.

113872.q: Which plant is the alkaloid morphine obtained from?
113872.e: Morphine comes from the milky sap of the opium poppy. It is a strong painkiller that only doctors may prescribe.
113872.m: The painkiller morphine is obtained from the opium poppy.

113873.q: Why must you not give chocolate to dogs?
a: It contains a substance that is poisonous to dogs
It makes dogs tired at once
113873.e: Cocoa contains the alkaloid theobromine. People break it down quickly, but dogs only very slowly, so it can poison them.

113874.q: Which bitter alkaloid from the bark of the cinchona tree helped against malaria?
113874.e: Quinine is obtained from the bark of the cinchona tree. For a long time it was the most important remedy against malaria, and it gives tonic water its bitter taste.
113874.m: Quinine from cinchona bark was long the most important malaria remedy.

113875.q: Which poisonous plant with shiny black berries contains the poison atropine?
113875.e: The scientific name of deadly nightshade is Atropa belladonna. The poison atropine gets its name from it.
113875.m: Deadly nightshade contains the poison atropine.

113876.e: Atropine is a strong poison found in deadly nightshade and other members of the nightshade family.

113877.q: Which part of the body does the poison atropine mainly affect?
113877.e: Atropine disrupts the passing on of signals in the nervous system. This changes things like the heartbeat, saliva and pupils.
113877.m: Atropine acts on the nervous system.

113878.q: Which plant family does deadly nightshade belong to?
113878.e: Like the potato, deadly nightshade belongs to the nightshade family. Many plants in this family contain poisons.
113878.m: Deadly nightshade belongs to the nightshade family.

113879.q: Why should you never eat unknown berries in the forest?
a: They could be poisonous like deadly nightshade
They make you tired at once
113879.e: Some berries, such as deadly nightshade, are deadly even in small amounts. That is why you only eat berries you know for certain.

113880.q: What should you do if someone has eaten deadly nightshade berries?
a: Call Tox Info on 145 or the emergency number at once
Get them to drink lots of milk
113880.e: Deadly nightshade poisoning is life-threatening. Tox Info Suisse on 145 and the emergency number 144 can help straight away.
113880.m: In case of poisoning, call 145 or 144 at once.

113881.q: Can a poison like atropine also be useful as a medicine?
a: Yes, in a small, exact dose
113881.e: In small, exactly measured amounts, doctors use atropine as a medicine, for example as an antidote to nerve poisons. The dose makes the poison.
113881.m: The dose decides whether a substance is poisonous or healing.

113882.q: What does “belladonna”, the species name of deadly nightshade, mean in Italian?
113882.e: In the past, women dripped deadly nightshade juice into their eyes. This made their pupils large, which was seen as beautiful. But it was dangerous.

113883.q: Besides deadly nightshade, which of these plants also contains atropine?
113883.e: The thorn apple is also a member of the nightshade family and contains poisons similar to deadly nightshade. Its seeds are especially poisonous.
113883.m: The thorn apple contains poisons similar to deadly nightshade.

113884.q: In which parts of monkshood is the poison especially concentrated?
a: In the hairs on the stem
113884.e: Aconitine is in all parts of the plant. But the root tubers and the seeds contain the most.
113884.m: In monkshood, the roots and seeds are especially poisonous.

113885.q: What amount of aconitine can already be deadly for an adult?
113885.e: Just about 5 milligrams of pure aconitine can kill an adult. That is a tiny amount, much less than a gram.
113885.m: Just a few milligrams of aconitine are life-threatening.

113886.q: Which Alpine plant contains the strong poison aconitine?
113886.e: Monkshood is considered the most poisonous plant in Europe. Its poison is called aconitine.

113887.q: What should you do if you see monkshood while hiking?
a: Do not pick it and do not touch it
113887.e: The poison of monkshood can even be taken in through the skin. So it is best to leave the plant where it is.

113888.q: Which first sign is typical of aconitine poisoning?
113888.e: Aconitine disrupts the nerves. First the mouth and skin tingle, and later the skin in these places goes numb.
113888.m: Monkshood poisoning often starts with tingling and numbness.

113889.q: Which plant family does monkshood belong to?
113889.e: Monkshood belongs to the buttercup family. There are many poisonous species in this family, including the buttercup itself.
113889.m: Monkshood belongs to the buttercup family.

113890.q: Where does the German name of monkshood, “Eisenhut” (iron hat), come from?
a: Its flower looks like a helmet
It only grows on iron ore
Its stems are as hard as iron
113890.e: The top petal arches like a knight's helmet, which used to be called an iron hat. That is where the name comes from. The English name monkshood compares it to a monk's hood.
113890.m: The monkshood flower looks like a helmet.

113891.q: Which organ can aconitine disrupt in a life-threatening way?
113891.e: Aconitine throws the heart rhythm into confusion and paralyses breathing. A person can die from this.
113891.m: Aconitine can throw the heart out of rhythm.

113892.q: Which plant contains the poison colchicine?
113892.e: The autumn crocus contains colchicine in all its parts. The seeds and the bulb are especially poisonous.
113892.m: The poison of the autumn crocus is called colchicine.

113893.q: Which edible plant are the poisonous leaves of the autumn crocus often confused with in spring?
