114714.e: Because large areas are never cleared, young, middle-aged and old trees stand mixed together. The forest stays permanently wooded and is resilient against disturbances.
114714.m: In a selection forest, young and old trees grow side by side.

114715.q: What does a forester do when thinning a forest?
a: She removes single trees so that the others grow better
She plants as many trees as possible close together
She counts the birds in the forest
She fertilises all the trees with artificial fertiliser
114715.e: When single trees are taken out, the remaining ones have more light, water and space. This makes them stronger and better able to withstand drought.
114715.m: Thinning gives the remaining trees more space.

114716.q: Which danger increases in hot, dry summers, especially south of the Alps and in Valais?
114716.e: Dry leaves and dead branches burn easily. That is why fire bans often apply in and near forests at such times.
114716.m: In dry summers the risk of forest fires rises.

114717.q: What does the WSL in Birmensdorf (Zurich) research?
114717.e: WSL stands for the Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research. Among other things, it studies how the forest reacts to climate change. The Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research SLF in Davos is also part of it.
114717.m: The WSL researches the Swiss forest.

114718.q: Why do foresters create small gaps in the forest when they want to encourage young oaks?
a: Oaks need lots of light to grow up
Oaks need wind for their roots
114718.e: Young oaks are light-loving trees and die in the shade of other trees. In open gaps they can establish themselves.
114718.m: Oaks need lots of light to grow up.

114719.q: What makes it hard for young oaks and silver firs to grow in many forests?
a: Browsing by roe deer and red deer
Too many fungi in the air
114719.e: Roe deer and red deer like to eat the buds of young oaks and silver firs. Yet these are exactly the species that matter for a forest fit for the future climate.
114719.m: Browsing by deer can stop important tree species from regrowing.

114720.q: Why are dead trees often left standing or lying in the forest today as deadwood?
a: It provides habitat for many species
It makes the soil rock hard
114720.e: Countless beetles, fungi, mosses and birds such as woodpeckers live in deadwood. A great variety of species makes the forest more stable against change.
114720.m: Deadwood is an important habitat in the forest.

114721.q: Which gas does a tree take from the air for photosynthesis?
114721.e: With light, water and carbon dioxide, the tree makes sugar. From this it builds wood, leaves and roots.
114721.m: Trees take carbon dioxide from the air to grow.

114722.q: What does it mean when a forest is a carbon sink?
a: It takes in more CO2 than it gives off
It gives off more CO2 than it takes in
It lies in a hollow in the valley
114722.e: A growing forest stores more carbon in wood and soil than is released through respiration and decay. So overall it removes CO2 from the air.
114722.m: A carbon sink stores more CO2 than it gives off.

114723.q: Roughly what proportion of dry wood is carbon?
114723.e: Wood consists mainly of cellulose and lignin. Around 50 per cent of its dry mass is carbon.
114723.m: Dry wood is about half carbon.

114724.q: A carbon atom weighs 12 units and an oxygen atom 16. How much carbon dioxide is produced when 12 kg of carbon burns completely?
114724.e: A CO2 particle weighs 12 + 2 times 16, so 44 units. That is why 12 kg of carbon becomes 44 kg of carbon dioxide.
114724.m: Burning carbon produces almost four times its mass in CO2.

114725.q: When can a forest become a source of carbon?
a: When many trees die and rot
When it comes into leaf in spring
114725.e: After storms, beetle attacks or fires, many dead trees decompose or burn. This releases more CO2 than the forest takes in at the same time.
114725.m: If a lot of forest dies, it gives off more CO2 than it takes in.

114726.q: How does the carbon from felled trees stay stored for an especially long time?
a: When the wood is used for houses and furniture
When the wood is burnt immediately
When the wood rots in the forest
When the wood becomes paper for one day
114726.e: In a wooden house or piece of furniture, the carbon often stays locked up for decades. Only when it rots or burns does it return to the air as CO2.
114726.m: Wood used in buildings stores carbon for a long time.

114727.q: Apart from the trees, where else in the forest is a great deal of carbon stored?
114727.e: A large amount of carbon is held in the humus and the roots. It comes from dead leaves, needles and wood.
114727.m: Forest soil is also a large carbon store.

114728.q: On the same area, which stores more carbon in total?
114728.e: In old forests, large amounts of carbon are held in thick trunks, deadwood and the soil. A young plantation first has to build up this store over many decades.
114728.m: Old forests are large carbon stores.

114729.q: With whom did the growing of sweet chestnuts spread widely in Central Europe?
114729.e: The Romans valued the sweet chestnut as food and as a source of wood. They also encouraged it to be grown in the Alpine valleys.
114729.m: The Romans encouraged the growing of sweet chestnuts.

114730.q: Why was the sweet chestnut once called the “bread tree” in Ticino?
a: Its fruits were an important staple food
Its bark was baked into bread
The bread oven stood under it
Its leaves were used as bread plates
114730.e: For many poor families in Ticino, chestnuts were the most important food for months. They were eaten fresh, dried or as flour.
114730.m: In Ticino, chestnuts once helped many families to survive.

114731.q: What is traditionally offered at chestnut festivals in autumn?
114731.e: Sweet chestnuts ripen in autumn. At chestnut festivals, for example in Fully in Valais or in Ticino, there are roasted chestnuts and other specialities.
114731.m: In autumn there are roasted chestnuts at chestnut festivals.

114732.q: Why were chestnuts once dried over smoke in Ticino?
a: So that they would keep for a long time
So that they became sweeter than sugar
114732.e: In small stone huts, the chestnuts lay on a rack over a low fire. Once dried, they kept through the winter.
114732.m: Dried chestnuts kept for a long time.

114733.q: Which fungal disease brought in from Asia badly damaged the chestnut trees in Ticino in the 20th century?
114733.e: The fungus forms wounds in the bark and makes branches die. Over time, however, weaker forms of the fungus appeared, so many trees survived.
114733.m: Chestnut blight is a dangerous fungal disease of the sweet chestnut.

114734.q: Which insect from China damages sweet chestnuts by forming growths on buds and leaves?
114734.e: The larvae of the gall wasp live in small growths called galls. Infested shoots produce fewer leaves and fruits.
114734.m: The gall wasp is a pest of the sweet chestnut.

114735.q: Which trees is the sweet chestnut closely related to?
114735.e: Like the beech and the oak, the sweet chestnut belongs to the beech family. Despite its similar name, it is not closely related to the horse chestnut.
114735.m: The sweet chestnut belongs to the beech family.

114736.q: What is the prickly case in which sweet chestnut fruits grow called?
114736.e: The nuts usually sit in twos or threes in a densely prickly cupule. In autumn it splits open and releases the chestnuts.
114736.m: Chestnuts ripen in a prickly cupule.

114737.q: Which sweet dish made from chestnut purée is popular in Switzerland in autumn?
114737.e: To make vermicelles, sweetened chestnut purée is pressed through a press into thin strands. They are often served with whipped cream.
114737.m: Vermicelles are made from chestnut purée.

114738.q: What is the aim of artificial intelligence?
a: Computers should solve tasks that otherwise need human thinking
Computers should use as little electricity as possible
Computers should work without a screen
Computers should connect to the internet faster
114738.e: Artificial intelligence (AI) tries to recreate abilities such as learning, understanding language or recognising images with computers. It uses programs and large amounts of data.
114738.m: Artificial intelligence lets computers solve tasks that need thinking.

114739.q: How do many AI programs learn?
a: From a huge amount of example data
114739.e: Many AI programs are trained with huge amounts of texts, images or numbers. From these, they recognise patterns.

114740.q: Roughly since when has there been research into artificial intelligence?
114740.e: In 1956, researchers met at Dartmouth College in the USA to talk about thinking machines. This meeting is seen as the start of AI research.

114742.q: What is true of almost all of today's AI systems?
a: They can do everything as well as a human
114742.e: An AI that plays chess usually cannot do anything else. An AI that could learn and understand everything like a human does not exist so far.
114742.m: Today's AI systems specialise in particular tasks.

114743.q: What are the neural networks used in AI?
a: Computer programs roughly modelled on the brain
114743.e: Neural networks consist of many connected computing units, similar to nerve cells in the brain. Important foundations for them were also developed at the IDSIA institute in Lugano.
114743.m: Neural networks are programs modelled on the brain.

114744.q: What is the name of the 2024 EU law that regulates the use of AI according to its risk?
114744.e: The AI Act sorts AI applications into risk classes. Particularly dangerous applications are banned, and strict rules apply to risky ones.
114744.m: The EU regulates AI according to its risk with the AI Act.

114745.q: What are deceptively real fake videos or voices made with AI called?
114745.e: With deepfakes, people can be made to say or do things that never happened. That is why you should check videos and audio recordings on the internet critically.
114745.m: Deepfakes are deceptively real fakes made with AI.

114746.q: What is the basic idea of machine learning?
a: The computer learns from books on the shelf
A person writes out every rule individually
114746.e: Instead of programming every rule by hand, the program recognises patterns in many examples. With what it has learned, it can then judge new cases.
114746.m: In machine learning, a computer recognises patterns in data.

114747.q: What is the learning method called in which the correct answer is given with each training example?
114747.e: In supervised learning, the model is given, for example, pictures labelled “dog” or “cat”. That way it learns to sort the pictures correctly itself.
114747.m: In supervised learning, the model knows the answer for each example.

114748.q: How does a program learn in reinforcement learning?
114748.e: The program tries out actions and receives points for good results. Over time, it chooses the actions that bring the most reward.
114748.m: In reinforcement learning, a program learns from rewards.

114749.q: What are artificial neural networks modelled on?
114749.e: Artificial neurons are greatly simplified copies of nerve cells. They are connected in layers and pass signals on.
114749.m: Neural networks are inspired by the brain.

114750.q: What does the word “deep” mean in deep learning?
a: The neural network has many layers
The computer is in the basement
114750.e: A deep neural network has many layers one after another. Each layer recognises slightly more complicated patterns than the one before.
114750.m: Deep learning uses neural networks with many layers.

114751.q: With which board game did an early computer program around 1959 show that a computer can learn from experience?
114751.e: At IBM, Arthur Samuel wrote a draughts program that got better and better over many games. In doing so, he coined the term “machine learning”.
114751.m: A draughts program gave machine learning its name.

114752.q: What is it called when a model learns the training examples by heart but does badly on new examples?
114752.e: In overfitting, the model remembers details instead of general patterns. That is why it fails with unfamiliar data.
114752.m: An overfitted model learns by heart instead of generalising.

114753.q: In unsupervised learning, what is it called when data is sorted into groups of similar things?
114753.e: In clustering, the program looks for groups itself, without anyone giving the correct answers. This way you can, for example, find customers with similar shopping habits.
114753.m: Clustering sorts data into groups of similar things.

114754.q: What was the simple learning machine called that Frank Rosenblatt presented in 1958?
114754.e: The perceptron is a very simple artificial neuron that can learn from examples. It is seen as a forerunner of today's neural networks.
114754.m: The perceptron is an early forerunner of neural networks.

114755.q: What was the famous early chatbot called that Joseph Weizenbaum developed in the 1960s?
114755.e: ELIZA was created around 1966 at MIT in the USA. The program reacted to keywords and so seemed surprisingly human.
114755.m: ELIZA was one of the first chatbots.

114756.q: What role did the early chatbot ELIZA play in its best-known version?
114756.e: ELIZA asked questions back and repeated what users said, as in a therapy session. Many people believed the program really understood them.

114757.q: When was the chatbot ChatGPT first made available to the public?
114757.e: ChatGPT was released by the US company OpenAI on 30 November 2022. Within a few weeks, millions of people were using it.
114757.m: ChatGPT has been publicly available since the end of 2022.

114759.q: What does a large language model basically do when it writes a text?
a: It predicts the most likely next piece of a word
It copies a finished text from a book
114759.e: The model calculates step by step which piece of a word fits best. Many such steps produce whole sentences.
114759.m: Language models create text one piece of a word at a time.

114760.q: What is it called when a chatbot gives convincing but made-up information?
114760.e: Language models produce plausible texts but do not automatically check whether they are true. That is why you should always check important information with reliable sources.
114760.m: Chatbots can make up false information, so you have to check it.

114761.q: What is the input or instruction you give a chatbot called?
114761.e: A prompt is the question or task you type in. The clearer the prompt, the better the answer usually fits.
114761.m: An instruction to a chatbot is called a prompt.

114762.q: What is the Turing test supposed to check?
a: Whether a machine seems like a human in conversation
Whether a computer has a virus
How much electricity a computer uses
114762.e: In the test, a person chats with a human and a machine. If they cannot reliably tell the two apart, the machine has passed.
114762.m: The Turing test checks whether a machine seems human.

114763.q: In which year did Alan Turing describe his test in a famous essay?
114763.e: In the essay “Computing Machinery and Intelligence”, Turing asked whether machines can think. Instead of an answer, he suggested a game as a test.

114764.q: What did Turing originally call his test?
114764.e: Turing spoke of the “imitation game” because the machine is supposed to imitate a human. Later the test was named after him.
114764.m: Turing called his test the imitation game.

114765.q: How do the participants communicate in the classic Turing test?
114765.e: So that appearance and voice give nothing away, communication only happens through keyboard and screen. Only what is written counts.
114765.m: In the Turing test, communication is only in writing.

114766.q: Which internet test checks the other way round whether a human and not a machine is sitting at the screen?
114766.e: With a CAPTCHA, you have to type in distorted letters or choose pictures, for example. The name contains the words “Turing test”.
114766.m: A CAPTCHA tells humans apart from programs.

114767.q: Which criticism is often made of the Turing test?
a: It only tests behaviour, not real understanding
114767.e: A machine could fool people without understanding what it writes. That is why the test says little about whether it really thinks.
114767.m: Seeming human does not mean really understanding.

114768.q: What was the name of a yearly competition in which chat programs tried to fool the judges?
114768.e: The Loebner Prize was awarded from 1991 for the most human chat program. It was based on the Turing test.
114768.m: The Loebner Prize was a competition modelled on the Turing test.

114769.q: When does a machine pass the Turing test?
a: When the questioner cannot reliably tell it apart from the human
When it solves all maths problems correctly
When it types faster than a human
When it knows a poem by heart
114769.e: What matters is not whether the answers are correct, but whether they seem human. The questioner has to guess who is human and who is the machine.
114769.m: In the Turing test, what counts is whether the machine seems human.

114770.q: Which country did the computer scientist Alan Turing come from?
114770.e: Alan Turing was born in London and studied in Cambridge. He is seen as one of the founders of computer science.
114770.m: Alan Turing was a British mathematician.

114771.q: Which German encryption machine did Turing help to crack in the Second World War?
114771.e: The German armed forces encrypted their radio messages with this machine. Turing developed methods to read the messages anyway.
114771.m: Turing helped to crack the Enigma.

114772.q: What happened at Bletchley Park, where Alan Turing worked, in the Second World War?
114772.e: At Bletchley Park, thousands of women and men worked in secret on decoding enemy radio messages. Today there is a museum there.
114772.m: At Bletchley Park, secret codes were cracked during the war.

114773.q: What is the imaginary computing model called that Turing described in 1936?
114773.e: The Turing machine reads and writes symbols on an infinitely long tape. With this simple model, you can work out what can be calculated at all.
114773.m: The Turing machine is a basic model of computer science.

114774.q: In which century did Alan Turing live?
114774.e: Alan Turing lived from 1912 to 1954. His ideas laid the foundations for today's computers.
114774.m: Alan Turing lived in the 20th century.

114775.q: What is the most important award in computer science, named after Turing, called?
114775.e: The Turing Award has been given every year since 1966. It is seen as the “Nobel Prize of computing”.
114775.m: The Turing Award is the best-known prize in computer science.

114776.q: What was the so-called Turing bombe used for in the Second World War?
114776.e: The Turing bombe was an electromechanical machine. It tested possible Enigma settings at high speed.
114776.m: The Turing bombe helped crack secret codes.

114777.q: Which subject did Alan Turing study at the University of Cambridge?
114777.e: Turing studied mathematics at King's College, Cambridge. His mathematical work laid the foundations for computers.
114777.m: Alan Turing was a mathematician by profession.

114778.q: What does a digital image consist of for a computer?
114778.e: A digital image is a grid of pixels. Each pixel stores its colour as numbers that a program can calculate with.
114778.m: For a computer, an image is a set of numbers.

114779.q: A colour image has 100 by 100 pixels, and each pixel stores three colour values. How many numbers is that?
114779.e: 100 times 100 gives 10,000 pixels. Times 3 colour values (red, green, blue), that makes 30,000 numbers.
114779.m: Even a small image consists of tens of thousands of numbers.

114780.q: Which type of neural network is especially good for image recognition?
114780.e: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) use small filters to look for edges, shapes and patterns in the image. Step by step, they build objects from simple patterns.
114780.m: Convolutional neural networks specialise in images.

114781.q: How does an AI learn to recognise cats in photos?
a: It practises with lots of example pictures of cats
It reads a book about cats
It asks a human for every picture
It can do it from the start without practice
114781.e: An AI is given thousands of pictures labelled with whether a cat can be seen. From them it learns typical patterns such as ears, fur and eyes.
114781.m: An AI learns to recognise images by seeing many examples.

114782.q: What is image recognition used for in medicine?
a: To find unusual signs on X-rays
114782.e: AI programs can, for example, check X-ray or skin images for suspicious areas. But the decision is still made by a doctor.
114782.m: Image recognition can support doctors in diagnosis.

114783.q: What is the technique called that lets a program recognise letters in a photographed text?
114783.e: Text recognition (OCR) turns images of letters into editable text. That way you can, for example, search a photo of a book page.
114783.m: Text recognition turns images of writing into real text.

114784.q: What can a plant identification app with image recognition do?
a: Suggest the plant species from a photo
114784.e: The app compares the photo with patterns it has learned from millions of plant pictures. The result is not always certain, especially with similar species.
114784.m: Image recognition can identify plants in photos.

114785.q: What is the task called in which an AI finds several objects in an image and marks them with boxes?
114785.e: In object detection, the AI says not only what is in the image but also where. Cameras in cars need this, for example, to find pedestrians.
114785.m: Object detection finds and marks objects in an image.

114786.q: Roughly since when have industrial robots been working in factories?
114786.e: The first industrial robot, Unimate, worked in a car factory in the USA from 1961. It moved hot metal parts.
114786.m: Industrial robots have existed since the 1960s.

114788.q: In which industry have industrial robots been welding and painting especially often for decades?
114788.e: In car factories, many robots work on assembly lines. They weld car bodies, paint and fit parts.
114788.m: Especially many robots work in car factories.

114789.q: What are robots called that work right next to people without a safety fence?
114789.e: Collaborative robots, or cobots for short, have sensors and stop when they touch a person. That way they can work hand in hand with people.
114789.m: Cobots work safely right next to people.

114791.q: What can be changed at the end of a robot arm depending on the task?
a: The tool, for example a gripper
114791.e: At the end of the arm there is a tool, the end effector. Depending on the task, it is a gripper, a welding device or a spray gun.
114791.m: A robot arm can carry different tools.

114792.q: Why do factories use industrial robots?
a: They work quickly, accurately and without breaks
114792.e: Robots repeat the same movement thousands of times very accurately. They also take over dangerous or heavy work.

114793.q: Which part of the human body is a typical industrial robot compared with?
114793.e: An articulated robot has joints like a shoulder, elbow and wrist. That is why it is also called a robot arm.
114793.m: An industrial robot works much like an arm.

114794.q: Which company developed the chess computer Deep Blue?
114794.e: Deep Blue was a special computer made by the American company IBM. It had chips built specially for chess.
114794.m: Deep Blue was a chess computer from IBM.

114795.q: Against which world chess champion did the computer Deep Blue win a six-game match?
114795.e: The Russian Garry Kasparov was the reigning world champion at the time. His defeat by a computer made headlines around the world.
114795.m: Garry Kasparov lost to Deep Blue as world champion.

114796.q: In which year did Deep Blue beat the reigning world chess champion?
114796.e: Deep Blue won the rematch against Garry Kasparov, which lasted from 3 to 11 May 1997. For IBM it was a huge publicity success.
114796.m: In 1997 a computer beat the world chess champion for the first time.

114797.q: How did the first match between Deep Blue and the world champion end in 1996?
114797.e: In 1996 Deep Blue did win one game, but lost the match overall. After that, the computer was greatly improved.
114797.m: In the first match in 1996, the human still won.

114798.q: In which city did Deep Blue's famous rematch take place?
114798.e: The match was held in 1997 in a skyscraper in Manhattan. Many spectators followed the games live.
114798.m: The famous rematch took place in New York.

114799.q: In 1997 Deep Blue won two games, lost one, and three ended in a draw. A draw counts as half a point. How many points did Deep Blue have?
114799.e: Two wins give 2 points, three draws 1.5 points. Together that makes 3.5 points; Kasparov got 2.5.
114799.m: Deep Blue won narrowly by 3.5 to 2.5 points.

114800.q: How did Deep Blue mainly find its moves?
a: By calculating many positions ahead at lightning speed
114800.e: Deep Blue checked about 200 million positions per second and rated them using rules set by humans. So it mainly used enormous computing power.
114800.m: Deep Blue won mainly thanks to enormous computing power.

114801.q: Why is Deep Blue's victory seen as a milestone in the history of AI?
a: For the first time a reigning world champion lost a match to a computer
For the first time a computer played chess at all
For the first time chess was shown on television
For the first time a woman won the world championship
114801.e: Chess was long seen as proof of human brainpower. A computer beating the best player changed the picture of what machines can do.
114801.m: Deep Blue's victory showed the strength of computers at chess.

114802.q: Which country does the board game Go originally come from?
114802.e: Go has been played in China for over 2500 years. Later it also became very popular in Japan and Korea.
114802.m: The board game Go comes from China.

114803.q: How many lines does a normal Go board have in each direction?
114803.e: On a Go board, 19 by 19 lines cross. The stones are placed on the 361 intersections.
114803.m: A Go board has 19 by 19 lines.

114804.q: Whom did the computer program AlphaGo beat in a famous match in 2016?
a: One of the best Go players in the world
114804.e: In Seoul, AlphaGo beat the South Korean Lee Sedol, one of the world's best Go players. Millions of people followed the match.
114804.m: In 2016 AlphaGo beat a top Go player.

114805.q: What was special about AlphaGo's victory in 2016?
a: For the first time a computer beat a top Go player
For the first time a computer played chess
For the first time Go was shown on television
For the first time children played Go
114805.e: Go was seen as especially difficult for computers. AlphaGo won four out of five games against Lee Sedol.
114805.m: AlphaGo was the first computer to beat a top Go player.

114806.e: DeepMind is an AI company from London that has belonged to Google since 2014. It later developed other programs such as AlphaFold.

114807.q: Why was Go long considered much harder than chess for computers?
a: There are many more possible courses of a game
Go is played without a board
114807.e: In Go there are a great many possible points for each move. So you cannot simply calculate all the options; you need something like intuition.
114807.m: Go has far more possibilities than chess.

114808.q: How did the version AlphaGo Zero, presented in 2017, learn the game?
a: Only by playing games against itself
114808.e: AlphaGo Zero only knew the rules and played millions of games against itself. After a few days it was stronger than the earlier version.
114808.m: AlphaGo Zero learned Go without any human games.

114809.q: Why did one of AlphaGo's moves in the second game against Lee Sedol become famous?
a: Professionals first thought it was a mistake, but it was brilliant
The computer needed a week for it
It ended the game after one move
114809.e: With move 37, AlphaGo placed a stone in an unusual spot. Later the move turned out to be brilliant.
114809.m: Move 37 is seen as an example of AlphaGo's creativity.

114810.q: Why does a self-driving car need many cameras and sensors?
114810.e: A self-driving car has to recognise roads, other vehicles, bikes and people. To do this, it combines cameras, radar and lasers.
114810.m: Self-driving cars recognise their surroundings with sensors.

114811.q: What does the highest level of driving automation mean?
a: The car drives anywhere entirely without a human
The car only keeps in its lane
The car only warns of dangers
114811.e: At the highest level, neither a steering wheel nor a driver is needed. Vehicles like this that can drive anywhere do not exist so far.
114811.m: Fully autonomous cars would drive anywhere without people.

114812.q: Which sensor scans the surroundings of a self-driving car with laser beams?
114812.e: A lidar sends out laser pulses and measures when they come back. This creates an accurate three-dimensional picture of the surroundings.
114812.m: A lidar measures distances with laser light.

114813.q: Which sensor uses radio waves and also works well in fog and rain?
114813.e: Radio waves pass through fog and rain better than light. That is why this sensor supports cameras and lasers.
114813.m: Radar can see even in bad weather.

114814.q: Where did driverless robot cars race in a famous contest from 2004?
a: Through a desert in the USA
114814.e: A US government agency had robot cars drive through the desert. In 2004 none reached the finish yet; in 2005 several made it.
114814.m: Desert races drove the development of self-driving cars.

114815.q: What was special about the car “Stanley”, which won a race through the desert in 2005?
a: It drove entirely without a driver
It ran only on solar power
114815.e: Stanley steered, braked and accelerated by itself. It drove the course of over 200 kilometres the fastest.
114815.m: Stanley was a robot car without a driver.

114816.q: In which Swiss town did PostBus test self-driving minibuses with passengers from 2016?
114816.e: The electric shuttles drove through the old town of Sion in Valais. It was one of the first trials of its kind in a public space.
114816.m: PostBus tested self-driving buses in Sion.

114817.q: What is a driver assistance system called that keeps the car in its lane?
114817.e: A camera recognises the lines on the road. If the car leaves the lane without meaning to, the system steers back slightly or gives a warning.
114817.m: Lane keeping assist keeps the car in its lane.

114818.q: What does a facial recognition system do?
a: It recognises people by their face
It puts make-up on faces on screen
It turns facial expressions into music
114818.e: The program compares a face with stored faces. If it finds a close enough match, it identifies the person.
114818.m: Facial recognition matches a face to a person.

114819.q: Which features does facial recognition measure, for example?
a: Distance between the eyes and shape of the nose
Length of the hair and colour of the clothes
114819.e: The position of and distances between eyes, nose, mouth and chin create a kind of number pattern of the face. This pattern is compared with others.
114819.m: Facial recognition compares distances and shapes in the face.

114820.q: What are methods called that recognise people by physical features such as their face or fingerprint?
114820.e: Biometric features are different in every person and can be measured. Besides the face and fingerprint, the iris in the eye is one of them.
114820.m: Biometrics recognises people by body features.

114821.q: What do many people use facial recognition for in everyday life?
114821.e: The smartphone recognises its owner's face and unlocks the device. Infrared sensors are often used for this.
114821.m: Many smartphones can be unlocked with your face.

114822.q: Why is facial recognition by cameras in public spaces controversial?
a: It can be used to watch lots of people
It makes the cameras too loud
114822.e: If you can be recognised everywhere, you lose some of your privacy. That is why its use is restricted by data protection rules in many countries.
114822.m: Facial recognition in public spaces affects data protection.

114823.q: Why did some facial recognition systems recognise people with dark skin less well?
a: The training images showed too few such faces
The programs were built that way on purpose
Dark skin has no facial features
114823.e: Studies showed that the training data mainly contained light-skinned faces. The system therefore learned unevenly well.
114823.m: One-sided data leads to unfair mistakes by AI.

114824.q: What does a camera do that marks faces with a frame and focuses on them when taking a photo?
a: It finds faces but does not know who they are
It recognises every person by name
It stores the faces in the passport
It compares faces with the police
114824.e: Finding a face in an image is called face detection. Only when the face is compared with stored data is a person identified.
114824.m: Finding a face is not the same as recognising it.

114825.q: Which biometric data is stored on the chip of a Swiss passport?
114825.e: Since 2010, the Swiss passport has contained two fingerprints as well as the facial image. This lets border staff check whether the passport belongs to the person.
114825.m: The Swiss passport contains a facial image and fingerprints.

114826.e: An AI model looks for patterns in the training data. The better and more varied this data is, the better the model works.
114826.m: An AI learns from its training data.

114827.q: What is labelling data called, for example putting “cat” under a picture of a cat?
114827.e: In annotation, people often add the correct label to each example. This work takes a lot of effort, but it is needed for many AI systems.
114827.m: Labelled data is called annotated data.

114828.q: Why is part of the data held back as test data when training an AI?
a: To check whether the AI can also solve unknown examples
So that the AI calculates faster
114828.e: If you trained and tested with the same data, the result would look too good. With held-back data, you can see whether the model really generalises.
114828.m: Test data shows how well an AI deals with new things.

114829.q: What does “bias” mean in training data?
a: The data shows reality in a one-sided way
114829.e: If the data contains distortions or prejudices, the AI takes them on. That is why training data must be chosen carefully.
114829.m: Biased data leads to biased AI results.

114830.q: What does the saying “garbage in, garbage out” mean in machine learning?
a: Bad data leads to bad results
Data must be deleted every day
114830.e: An AI cannot be better than the data it learns from.

114831.q: What do the images in the well-known practice data set MNIST show?
114831.e: MNIST contains 70,000 small images of the handwritten digits 0 to 9. Many people use it to train their first neural network.
114831.m: MNIST is a well-known data set of handwritten digits.

114832.q: Why does an AI need millions of labelled images for image recognition?
a: So that the computer looks nicer
So that nobody can copy the AI
114832.e: An AI only recognises patterns once it has seen many examples. The image database ImageNet, with over 14 million labelled images, greatly advanced image recognition.
114832.m: An AI needs many labelled examples.

114833.q: Which legal question arises when AI is trained with texts and images from the internet?
114833.e: Many texts and images belong to authors, artists or publishers. Whether they may be used for training without permission is disputed in many countries.
114833.m: Training AI raises the question of copyright.

114834.q: Who is known as the “father of medicine”?
114834.e: The Greek doctor Hippocrates is seen as the founder of scientific medicine. He explained illnesses by natural causes instead of the anger of the gods.
114834.m: Hippocrates is called the father of medicine.

114835.q: What is the promise called that is named after Hippocrates and describes a doctor's duties?
114835.e: In the oath, a doctor promises among other things to help the sick and not to harm them. It is still a model for medical ethics today.
114835.m: The Hippocratic Oath describes the duties of doctors.

114836.q: How did medicine explain illnesses for a long time after Hippocrates?
a: As an imbalance of the body's fluids
114836.e: According to the theory of the four humours, we are made of blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. If their balance is upset, you become ill. This theory was accepted until the 19th century.
114836.m: The old theory of the four humours explained illness as an imbalance of body fluids.

114837.q: Which diet and way of life did Hippocratic medicine often recommend as the first treatment?
a: Eating in moderation, rest and exercise
Lots of meat and little sleep
Only water and no food at all
114837.e: Hippocratic doctors relied first on diet, meaning a healthy way of life with suitable food, rest and exercise. Only after that did they turn to medicines or operations.
114837.m: Hippocratic medicine relied on a healthy way of life.

114838.q: What was especially important to Hippocrates when treating patients?
114838.e: Hippocrates observed the sick carefully and wrote down how the illness developed. That was an important step towards scientific medicine.
114838.m: Hippocrates relied on careful observation of the sick.

114839.q: Where did the doctor Hippocrates come from?
114839.e: Hippocrates lived on the Greek island of Kos. He and his students wrote many medical books.
114839.m: Hippocrates was a doctor from ancient Greece.

114840.q: Roughly in which century did Hippocrates live?
114840.e: Hippocrates was born around 460 BC and died around 370 BC. So he lived during the Classical period of Greece.
114840.m: Hippocrates lived in the 5th century BC.

114841.q: In which present-day Swiss canton was the doctor Paracelsus born?
114841.e: Paracelsus was born around 1493 in Egg near Einsiedeln. Einsiedeln is in the canton of Schwyz.
114841.m: Paracelsus was born near Einsiedeln in the canton of Schwyz.

114842.q: Which famous saying about poisons goes back to Paracelsus?
114842.e: Paracelsus realised that almost any substance is harmful in too large an amount and can be harmless or even healing in a small amount. The amount is what matters.
114842.m: According to Paracelsus, the dose makes the poison.

114844.q: In which Swiss city was Paracelsus the city doctor in 1527 and taught at the university?
114844.e: Paracelsus became city doctor in Basel in 1527 and gave lectures at the university. After quarrels with colleagues he had to leave the city as early as 1528.
114844.m: Paracelsus was city doctor in Basel around 1527.

114845.q: What was unusual about Paracelsus's lectures in Basel?
a: He spoke German instead of Latin
He only read from the Bible
114845.e: Scholars taught in Latin at that time. Paracelsus gave his lectures in German so that more people could understand him.
114845.m: Paracelsus taught in German instead of Latin.

114846.q: Which science did Paracelsus combine with medicine by making remedies from minerals and metals?
114846.e: Paracelsus used chemical methods to make medicines from minerals and metals. That is why he is seen as a pioneer of modern pharmacology.

114847.q: In which century did Paracelsus work?
114847.e: Paracelsus lived from about 1493 to 1541. So his work falls in the first half of the 16th century, at the time of the Reformation.

114848.q: Which country did the doctor Edward Jenner come from?
114848.e: Edward Jenner was an English country doctor from Berkeley in the county of Gloucestershire. That is where he carried out his famous experiments.
114848.m: Edward Jenner was an English country doctor.

114849.q: Against which disease did Edward Jenner develop the first vaccination?
114849.e: Jenner passed on material from a related, harmless germ and so protected people against the dangerous disease. His method spread quickly throughout Europe.
114849.m: Jenner developed the first vaccination against smallpox.

114850.q: In which century did Edward Jenner carry out the first smallpox vaccination?
114850.e: Jenner vaccinated against smallpox for the first time in 1796, so at the end of the 18th century. His method spread quickly in Europe.
114850.m: The first smallpox vaccination took place at the end of the 18th century.

114851.q: Which harmless germ did Edward Jenner use to vaccinate against dangerous smallpox?
114851.e: Cowpox is mild in humans but protects against real smallpox. Jenner took the material from a blister of an infected woman.

114852.q: Which disease is now considered wiped out worldwide thanks to vaccinations?
114852.e: After worldwide vaccination campaigns, the WHO declared smallpox eradicated in 1980. It all began with Jenner's vaccination.
114852.m: Smallpox was wiped out thanks to vaccinations.

114853.q: Where does the word “vaccination” come from?
a: From the Latin word for cow
From the Greek word for needle
From the Latin word for blood
From the English word for protection
114853.e: The Latin word “vacca” means cow. The name is a reminder of where the first vaccine came from.
114853.m: The word vaccination comes from the Latin word for cow.

114854.q: What did Edward Jenner notice about milkmaids in the countryside?
a: They did not get smallpox after having cowpox
They were never bitten by mosquitoes
114854.e: People knew that milkmaids were protected against smallpox after the harmless cowpox. Jenner tested this observation scientifically.
114854.m: Jenner's idea began with an observation of milkmaids.

114855.q: What is Jenner often called because of his groundbreaking work?
114855.e: Jenner's smallpox vaccination was the first scientifically tested vaccination. It laid the foundation for all later vaccines.
114855.m: Edward Jenner is known as the father of vaccination.

114856.q: Which country did Louis Pasteur come from?
114856.e: Louis Pasteur was born in 1822 in Dole in eastern France. He was a chemist and microbiologist.
114856.m: Louis Pasteur was a French scientist.

114857.q: What is the process called in which milk is heated briefly to kill germs?
114857.e: In pasteurisation, milk is heated briefly to about 72 to 75 degrees. Most germs die, but the taste stays almost the same.
114857.m: Pasteurisation is named after Louis Pasteur.

114858.q: Against which disease did Louis Pasteur successfully use a vaccine on a human for the first time in 1885?
114858.e: In 1885 Pasteur treated a boy who had been bitten by a rabid dog. The boy survived thanks to the vaccination.
114858.m: In 1885 Pasteur vaccinated a human against rabies for the first time.

114859.q: What was the name of the boy Louis Pasteur treated for rabies in 1885?
114859.e: Joseph Meister was nine years old and came from Alsace. He later worked as a caretaker at the Pasteur Institute.
114859.m: The first boy treated for rabies was called Joseph Meister.

114860.q: Which old idea did Louis Pasteur disprove using glass flasks with a long, curved neck?
a: That life arises by itself from dead matter
That light is made of particles
114860.e: In his swan-neck flasks, a boiled nutrient liquid stayed free of germs because dust and germs got stuck in the curved neck. So life only comes from life.
114860.m: Pasteur showed that life does not arise by itself from dead matter.

114861.q: What is the famous research institute called that Louis Pasteur founded in Paris in 1887?
114861.e: The Pasteur Institute was founded in 1887 and opened in 1888. It still researches infectious diseases and vaccines today.
114861.m: The Pasteur Institute in Paris goes back to Louis Pasteur.

114862.q: Which living things did Louis Pasteur identify as the cause of fermentation, for example in wine and beer?
114862.e: Pasteur showed that living microorganisms such as yeast cause fermentation. Before that, fermentation was thought to be a purely chemical process.
114862.m: Pasteur realised that microorganisms cause fermentation.

114863.q: Against which animal disease did Pasteur develop a vaccine for sheep and cattle in 1881?
114863.e: In 1881 Pasteur proved in a public experiment that vaccinated sheep survived anthrax. Unvaccinated animals died.
114863.m: Pasteur developed a vaccine against anthrax in 1881.

114864.q: Which present from his wife allowed the young country doctor Robert Koch to start his research?
114864.e: Koch's wife Emmy gave him a microscope. With it he examined blood samples and bacteria in his practice.
114864.m: A microscope from his wife was the start of Koch's research.

114865.q: Which country did the doctor Robert Koch come from?
114865.e: Robert Koch was born in 1843 in Clausthal in the Harz mountains. He later worked mainly in Berlin.
114865.m: Robert Koch was a German doctor and researcher.

114866.q: Which day of remembrance recalls Koch's discovery every year on 24 March?
114866.e: On 24 March 1882 Koch announced the discovery of the germ that causes tuberculosis. That is why this day is now World Tuberculosis Day.

114867.q: Which prize did Robert Koch receive in 1905?
114867.e: In 1905 Koch received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. It honoured his research on a serious infectious disease.
114867.m: Robert Koch received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1905.

114868.q: What did Robert Koch prove as one of the first people?
a: That blood circulates in the body
That the Earth goes round the Sun
114868.e: In 1876, using anthrax as an example, Koch showed that a particular bacterium causes a particular disease. That was a milestone in medicine.
114868.m: Koch proved that bacteria cause diseases.

114869.q: Which dangerous diarrhoeal disease often spreads through dirty drinking water?
114869.e: Cholera is spread by bacteria in dirty water. Robert Koch found the germ in India in 1884.
114869.m: Clean drinking water protects against cholera.

114870.q: What is the health institute in Berlin called that is named after Robert Koch?
114870.e: The Robert Koch Institute is Germany's central authority for infectious diseases. Koch was the institute's first director.
114870.m: The Robert Koch Institute in Berlin bears Koch's name.

114871.q: What did Robert Koch test with his famous rules?
a: Whether a germ causes a particular disease
114871.e: According to Koch's rules, a germ must be found in every sick person, be grown in a pure culture and cause the same disease in a healthy animal. They are called Koch's postulates.
114871.m: Koch's rules are used to test whether a germ causes a disease.

114872.q: Why was penicillin produced in large amounts during the Second World War?
a: To treat infected wounds of the injured
114872.e: In the past many wounded people died of wound infections caused by bacteria. With penicillin, these infections could be treated effectively for the first time.
114872.m: Penicillin saved many injured people in the Second World War.

114873.q: Where does penicillin originally come from?
114873.e: Penicillin is made by moulds of the genus Penicillium. They use it to kill bacteria around them.

114874.q: Which group of medicines does penicillin belong to?
114874.e: Antibiotics kill bacteria or stop them from growing. Penicillin was one of the first antibiotics.

114875.q: Which germs does penicillin work against, and which not?
114875.e: Penicillin attacks the cell wall of bacteria. Viruses do not have such a cell wall, so it does not help against flu, for example.
114875.m: Antibiotics help against bacteria but not against viruses.

114876.q: In which field did Alexander Fleming receive the Nobel Prize?
114876.e: Fleming received the Nobel Prize in Medicine together with two researchers from Oxford. It honoured the discovery of penicillin and its use as a medicine.
114876.m: Fleming received the Nobel Prize in Medicine.

114877.q: How did Fleming come to discover penicillin?
a: By chance, with a mouldy culture dish
Through a tip from a farmer
On an expedition to the jungle
114877.e: After his holiday, Fleming found a culture dish on which mould had grown. Around the mould the bacteria had died.
114877.m: Fleming discovered penicillin by a lucky accident.

114878.q: Why should you not take an antibiotic unnecessarily or incorrectly?
a: Because bacteria can otherwise become resistant
Because it otherwise turns into viruses
114878.e: If antibiotics are used wrongly or too often, tough bacteria survive and multiply. Then antibiotics no longer work.

114879.q: Which rays did Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen discover in 1895?
114879.e: Röntgen called the unknown rays “X-rays”. In German-speaking countries they are now called Röntgen rays after him.

114880.q: Which country did Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen come from?
114880.e: Röntgen was a German physicist. He studied in Zurich and in 1895 discovered the rays named after him in Germany.

114881.q: What did the famous first X-ray image of a person show?
114881.e: At the end of 1895 Röntgen X-rayed the hand of his wife Anna Bertha. The picture shows the bones and her ring.
114881.m: The first famous X-ray image shows the hand of Röntgen's wife.

114882.q: Which famous award did Röntgen receive in 1901 as the very first physicist?
114882.e: The Nobel Prizes were awarded for the first time in 1901. Röntgen received the Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering X-rays.
114882.m: Röntgen received the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901.

114883.q: At which Swiss university did Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen study?
114883.e: Röntgen studied mechanical engineering at the Zurich Polytechnic, today's ETH. Later he gained his doctorate at the University of Zurich.

114884.q: What can X-rays make especially easy to see?
114884.e: X-rays pass through soft tissue more easily than through bone. That is why bones appear light on the picture.
114884.m: Bones show up especially well on X-ray images.

114885.q: Why did Röntgen earn hardly any money from his discovery?
a: He sold it to the emperor
114885.e: Röntgen wanted his discovery to benefit everyone. That is why he did not take out a patent.
114885.m: Röntgen did not patent his discovery.

114886.q: Why do patients sometimes wear a lead apron when having an X-ray?
a: It protects parts of the body from the rays
114886.e: In large amounts, X-rays can damage cells. Lead blocks the rays well and so protects parts of the body that are not being examined.
114886.m: A lead apron protects against unnecessary rays during an X-ray.

114887.q: What is Florence Nightingale mainly known for?
a: As the founder of modern nursing
As the inventor of the clinical thermometer
114887.e: Florence Nightingale made nursing a respected profession with proper training. She placed great importance on cleanliness and fresh air.
114887.m: Florence Nightingale is seen as the founder of modern nursing.

114888.q: Besides nursing, in which field was Florence Nightingale also very gifted?
114888.e: Florence Nightingale collected figures and showed them in diagrams. In this way she showed how important cleanliness is in hospitals.
114888.m: Florence Nightingale used numbers to save lives.

114889.q: In which city was Florence Nightingale born, which also gave her her first name?
114889.e: She was born in Florence in 1820 while her parents were travelling. Her first name is the English form of the city's name.
114889.m: Florence Nightingale is named after her birthplace, Florence.

114890.q: Which international day is celebrated on 12 May, Florence Nightingale's birthday?
114890.e: Florence Nightingale was born on 12 May 1820. That is why nursing professions are honoured worldwide on this day.

114891.q: What did Florence Nightingale use to convince politicians of better hygiene?
114891.e: She collected figures on the causes of soldiers' deaths and drew clear diagrams from them. These showed that many died of avoidable diseases.
114891.m: Florence Nightingale convinced people with statistics and diagrams.

114892.q: What did most soldiers die of in the military hospital at Scutari before Nightingale's improvements?
114892.e: More soldiers died of diseases such as typhus and cholera than of their injuries. Dirt, bad water and cramped rooms helped the diseases spread.
114892.m: Most soldiers in the military hospital died of infections.

114893.q: Which Swiss city did Henry Dunant come from?
114893.e: Henry Dunant was born in Geneva on 8 May 1828. The Red Cross was later founded in Geneva as well.

114894.q: Which battle in Italy did Henry Dunant witness in 1859, after which he helped the wounded?
114894.e: At Solferino, thousands of wounded were left lying without help. Dunant organised their care with women from the village of Castiglione.
114894.m: Dunant witnessed the Battle of Solferino in 1859.

114895.q: Which aid organisation goes back to Henry Dunant?
114895.e: After what he saw on the battlefield of Solferino, Dunant worked for neutral help for the wounded. In 1863 the Red Cross was founded in Geneva.
114895.m: Henry Dunant is the founder of the Red Cross.

114896.q: Which international agreement to protect wounded soldiers was signed in Geneva in 1864?
114896.e: At the suggestion of the new committee in Geneva, twelve states signed the first Geneva Convention in 1864. It protects the wounded and medical staff in war.
114896.m: The first Geneva Convention of 1864 protects the wounded in war.

114897.q: Which prize did Henry Dunant receive in 1901 as one of the first winners?
114897.e: Dunant shared the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901 with the Frenchman Frédéric Passy. At that time he was living poor and withdrawn.
114897.m: Henry Dunant received the first Nobel Peace Prize in 1901.

114898.q: Which day is celebrated on 8 May, Henry Dunant's birthday?
114898.e: On 8 May, Red Cross and Red Crescent societies around the world celebrate their founder. The day recalls the work of the helpers.
114898.m: 8 May is World Red Cross Day.

114899.q: Where are smallpox viruses still officially kept today?
a: In two high-security laboratories in the USA and Russia
In every hospital in the world
Nowhere in the world any more
114899.e: After smallpox ended, almost all virus samples were destroyed. Only two closely guarded laboratories in the USA and in Russia may still store samples.
114899.m: Smallpox viruses are officially stored in only two laboratories.

114900.q: Why was it possible to defeat smallpox completely?
a: The virus only infects humans, not animals
The virus dies out in winter
The virus only lives in water
114900.e: Because the smallpox virus only survives in humans, it could not hide anywhere. When everyone around a case was vaccinated, the chain of infection was broken.
114900.m: Smallpox could be defeated because the virus only infects humans.

114901.q: What kind of germ causes smallpox?
114901.e: Smallpox is caused by a very small disease particle that can only multiply in living cells. It is passed from person to person.
114901.m: Smallpox is caused by a virus.

114902.q: What did many people who had survived smallpox keep?
a: Scars on the face and skin
114902.e: Smallpox forms blisters filled with fluid on the skin. When they heal, they often leave deep scars.
114902.m: Smallpox often left scars on the skin.

114903.q: Where did the material for the first smallpox vaccination come from?
114903.e: The English doctor Edward Jenner used harmless cowpox for vaccination in 1796. The word vaccine comes from the Latin “vacca” for cow.
114903.m: The first smallpox vaccination came from cowpox.

114904.q: Why do people in Switzerland no longer need to be vaccinated against smallpox?
a: Because the disease has been wiped out
Because it can be cured with tea
Because smallpox only occurs in the tropics
114904.e: There have been no smallpox cases for decades, so the vaccination is no longer needed. General smallpox vaccination has therefore been stopped worldwide.
114904.m: People are no longer vaccinated against smallpox because it has been wiped out.

114905.e: The smallpox virus was passed on through coughing, talking or the blisters. That is why mainly people close to the sick were infected.
114905.m: Smallpox spread from person to person.

114906.q: By what name is the great wave of plague in Europe in the 14th century known?
114906.e: The pandemic in the 14th century is called the Black Death. It was one of the worst epidemics in history.
114906.m: The great plague of the 14th century is called the Black Death.

114907.q: Which animals spread the plague with their fleas?
114907.e: Fleas on rats carried the plague germ. When the fleas bit people, they infected them.

114908.q: How did the Black Death reach Europe?
a: On the wind from the desert
114908.e: Trading ships from the Black Sea brought the plague to Sicily. From there it spread across the whole of Europe.
114908.m: Trading ships brought the plague to Europe.

114909.q: Roughly what share of Europe's population died of the Black Death in the 14th century?
114909.e: Estimates suggest around 25 million deaths. That was about a third of Europe's population at the time.
114909.m: The Black Death killed about a third of the people in Europe.

114910.q: Where does the word “quarantine” come from?
a: From the Italian word for forty days
From the Latin word for illness
From the French word for harbour
From the Greek word for fear
114910.e: In Venice, ships from plague areas had to wait 40 days before anyone was allowed ashore. In Italian, forty is “quaranta”.

114911.q: What kind of germ causes the plague?
114911.e: The plague germ is a rod-shaped bacterium. Because it is a bacterium, plague can be treated with antibiotics today.
114911.m: The plague is caused by a bacterium.

114912.q: What did some plague doctors wear on their faces in the 17th century?
a: A mask with a long beak
114912.e: The beak was filled with sweet-smelling herbs. At that time people believed the plague was spread by bad air.
114912.m: Plague doctors wore masks with long beaks.

114913.q: Which form of plague occurs when the germ attacks the lungs and is passed on by coughing?
114913.e: In pneumonic plague, the bacteria get into the air when someone coughs. In this way it can be passed directly from person to person.
114913.m: Pneumonic plague is passed on by coughing.

114914.q: How can you recognise bubonic plague?
a: By green spots on the tongue
114914.e: In bubonic plague, the lymph nodes, for example in the armpit or neck, swell into painful lumps. That is where its name comes from.
114914.m: Bubonic plague shows itself through swollen lymph nodes.

114915.q: Which simple measure did Ignaz Semmelweis introduce in a Vienna hospital in 1847?
114915.e: Semmelweis demanded that doctors and students disinfect their hands before examinations. After that the number of deaths fell sharply.

114916.q: What happened after Semmelweis introduced hand disinfection?
114916.e: After it was introduced, the number of deaths in his ward fell sharply. That showed how important clean hands are.
114916.m: Thanks to hand disinfection, far fewer patients died.

114917.q: In which city was Ignaz Semmelweis working when he made his discovery?
114917.e: Semmelweis was an assistant doctor at the General Hospital in Vienna. There he compared the death rates of two wards.
114917.m: Semmelweis made his discovery in Vienna.

114918.q: In which century did Ignaz Semmelweis live?
114918.e: Semmelweis lived from 1818 to 1865. He made his discovery in Vienna in 1847.

114919.q: According to Semmelweis, where did the doctors bring the dangerous germs onto the ward from?
114919.e: Many doctors examined patients straight after dissecting dead bodies. Without washing their hands, they passed on deadly germs.
114919.m: The germs came from dead bodies on the doctors' hands.

114920.q: How did many doctors react to Semmelweis's demands at the time?
a: They made him the emperor's doctor
They gave him the Nobel Prize
114920.e: Many colleagues did not want to believe that their own hands spread diseases. Only after his death in 1865 were his ideas accepted.
114920.m: During his lifetime Semmelweis was rejected by many doctors.

114921.q: What did people not yet know at the time of Semmelweis, around 1847?
a: That water is needed for life
114921.e: It was only decades later that scientists proved bacteria cause diseases. So Semmelweis could not explain exactly why handwashing helped.
114921.m: Semmelweis worked before bacteria were known to cause disease.

114922.q: Why is Semmelweis seen today as a role model for hospital hygiene?
a: He showed that clean hands save lives
114922.e: His figures proved that the death rate fell sharply after hand disinfection was introduced. Hand hygiene is today the most important measure against hospital infections.
114922.m: Semmelweis showed that clean hands save lives.

114923.q: What is the flat glass dish for bacterial cultures called, invented by an assistant of Robert Koch?
114923.e: Julius Petri worked in Koch's laboratory in Berlin and developed the flat dish with a lid in 1887. It is still used in laboratories all over the world today.
114923.m: The Petri dish comes from Robert Koch's laboratory.

114924.q: In which city was Alexander Fleming working when he discovered penicillin?
114924.e: Fleming did research at St Mary's Hospital in London. Today there is a small museum in his former laboratory.

114925.q: What does a doctor promise in the medical oath, among other things?
a: To earn as much money as possible
114925.e: Since Hippocrates, doctors have promised to act for the good of the sick and not to harm them. Today there is a modern version, the Declaration of Geneva.
114925.m: Doctors promise not to harm the sick.

114926.q: In which test facility do cycling and ski teams measure the air resistance of their athletes?
114926.e: In a wind tunnel a large fan blows air past the person, who stays still. Sensors measure the braking force, so position and equipment can be improved.
114926.m: Air resistance is measured in a wind tunnel.

114927.q: Why do Formula 1 cars have big wings at the front and back?
a: They press the car onto the track
They make the car take off
114927.e: The wings are shaped the opposite way to an aeroplane's. They create downforce, so the car grips better and can go faster through corners.
114927.m: The wings of a racing car create downforce.

114928.q: Why are sprint and cycling records often easier to set in places high above sea level?
a: The thinner air slows you down less
There is no gravity there at all
114928.e: High up, the air density is lower. So air resistance falls, even though breathing is harder.
114928.m: In thin mountain air, air resistance is lower.

114929.q: What are the many small dimples on a golf ball for?
114929.e: The dimples create a thin, swirling layer of air around the ball. The air therefore separates later, the wake behind the ball gets smaller and the ball flies further.
114929.m: Dimples make a golf ball fly further.

114930.q: Why do cyclists in time trials wear helmets with a long, pointed shape?
a: So the air flows off better
114930.e: A streamlined shape lets the air flow smoothly back together behind the head. This creates fewer braking swirls.
114930.m: Streamlined helmets let the air flow off smoothly.

114931.q: What kind of bicycle wheel is often used at the back on the track to avoid air swirls from the spokes?
a: A wheel with twice as many spokes
114931.e: Spinning spokes churn up the air and slow you down. A closed disc wheel has no spokes and creates less resistance.
114931.m: Disc wheels reduce the air swirls from spokes.

114932.q: Which science studies how air flows around moving objects?
114932.e: The Greek word ‘aer’ means air. Aerodynamics studies air flows and the forces they put on objects.
114932.m: Aerodynamics studies how air flows around objects.

114933.q: Why are the racing suits of speed skaters and skiers very tight and smooth?
a: So the air slows them down less
So you can put them on faster
114933.e: Flapping fabric and folds create swirls and increase air resistance. Smooth, tight suits let the air flow past better.
114933.m: Tight, smooth suits reduce air resistance.

114934.q: Why is it forbidden in many triathlons to ride closely behind someone else on the bike course?
a: Because the slipstream gives an unfair advantage
Because the roads are too narrow
Because the bikes would have to crash
Because you would get too slow
114934.e: Anyone riding in the slipstream saves a lot of energy for the run that follows. That is why athletes in such races must keep a minimum distance.
114934.m: In many triathlons, riding in the slipstream is forbidden.

114935.q: In a group of cyclists, who has to work hardest against air resistance?
114935.e: The rider at the front meets the undisturbed air. The others ride in his slipstream.
114935.m: Air resistance is greatest at the front.

114936.q: Why do cyclists in a breakaway group take turns at the front?
a: So everyone can recover in the slipstream
So everyone is photographed equally often
So the bikes don't get hot
114936.e: Working at the front is tiring. By taking turns the effort is shared, and the group stays faster overall.
114936.m: Taking turns shares the work at the front.

114937.q: What do racing drivers use the slipstream of a car in front for?
114937.e: In the slipstream the resistance is lower, so the car behind gets faster. With this extra speed it then pulls out and passes.
114937.m: Racing drivers use the slipstream to overtake.

114938.q: What is a runner called who sets the pace at the front during record attempts and provides a slipstream?
114938.e: Pacemakers run a set distance at an even pace in front of the favourites. They can shelter from the wind behind them.

114939.q: Which runner, helped by many pacemakers, became the first person to run a marathon in under two hours, in Vienna in 2019?
114939.e: Eliud Kipchoge ran 1:59:40 in Vienna in October 2019. Because the pacemakers changed during the run, the time does not count as an official world record.
114939.m: Kipchoge ran a marathon in under two hours in 2019.

114940.q: Why does the slipstream hardly matter for people walking slowly?
a: Because air resistance is very small at low speed
Because there is only a slipstream when it is windy
Because people don't create a slipstream
Because the air is warmer when walking
114940.e: Air resistance depends strongly on speed. Only at higher speeds, for example on a bike, is riding in the slipstream clearly worth it.
114940.m: The slipstream is worth it mainly at high speed.

114941.q: In which formation do large migrating birds often fly to save energy?
a: Stacked on top of each other
114941.e: Behind a bird's wingtips the air rises slightly. The birds behind use this updraught and save energy.
114941.m: Migrating birds save energy in a V formation.

114942.q: Apart from speed and the radius of the curve, what else does centrifugal force depend on?
114942.e: Centrifugal force is proportional to mass. An object twice as heavy is pushed outwards twice as strongly in the same curve.
114942.m: The greater the mass, the greater the centrifugal force.

114943.q: A car drives fast round a bend. Which way are the passengers pushed?
a: Towards the centre of the bend
114943.e: Because of its inertia, the body wants to keep going straight. But the car turns into the bend, so you feel pushed outwards. This effect is called centrifugal force.
114943.m: In a bend you feel the centrifugal force pushing outwards.

114944.q: Centrifugal force grows with the square of the speed. How does it change if you go round the same bend twice as fast?
a: It becomes four times as big
114944.e: You work out 2 squared, so 2 times 2. That gives 4. That is why going round bends too fast is so dangerous.
114944.m: Double the speed means four times the centrifugal force.

114945.q: At the same speed, how does the centrifugal force change when a bend gets tighter?
114945.e: Centrifugal force is inversely proportional to the radius of the bend. The tighter the bend, the more strongly you are pushed outwards.
114945.m: In tight bends the centrifugal force is greater.

114946.q: Which kitchen gadget uses centrifugal force to separate water from washed salad?
114946.e: In the fast-spinning spinner, the water flies outwards through the holes in the basket. The salad stays in the basket.
114946.m: The salad spinner separates water using centrifugal force.

114947.q: Why do the seats on a chair swing ride swing out at an angle?
a: Because of the centrifugal force as it turns
Because the chains are too long
114947.e: As it turns, centrifugal force pulls the seats outwards and gravity pulls them down. Together this gives a slanted position.
114947.m: On a chair swing ride, centrifugal force pushes the seats outwards.

114948.q: Why doesn't the water fall out when you swing a bucket quickly in a circle over your head?
a: Because the spinning presses it into the bucket
Because water sticks to the bucket
Because the air holds the water
114948.e: With enough speed, the effect of the spinning at the top is greater than gravity. The water is pressed against the bottom of the bucket.
114948.m: When spun fast, the water stays in the bucket.

114949.q: What is the lab device called that separates substances by their density by spinning very fast?
114949.e: In a centrifuge, heavier parts are pushed outwards more strongly than lighter ones. This is how, for example, blood cells are separated from blood plasma.
114949.m: A centrifuge separates substances by spinning fast.

114950.q: In which direction does the centripetal force point in circular motion?
a: Towards the centre of the circle
114950.e: The word comes from the Latin ‘centrum’ for centre and ‘petere’ for to seek. The force constantly pulls the object towards the centre.
114950.m: The centripetal force points towards the centre of the circle.

114951.q: In the hammer throw, what happens to the hammer as soon as the thrower lets go?
a: It flies off along a tangent
It keeps going round in a circle
114951.e: After letting go, the force that kept it on its circular path is gone. The hammer flies in the direction it was moving at that moment, that is, along a tangent.
114951.m: Without centripetal force, an object flies off along a tangent.

114952.q: In the hammer throw, what provides the centripetal force for the spinning hammer?
a: The steel wire the thrower pulls on
114952.e: The thrower holds the hammer by the wire and pulls it towards the centre. This keeps the ball on its circular path.
114952.m: In the hammer throw, the wire keeps the hammer on its circular path.

114953.q: What provides the centripetal force needed for a bicycle on a flat bend?
a: The friction between tyres and road
114953.e: The tyres press sideways against the road, and the grip acts towards the centre of the bend. On ice this friction is missing, which is why you slip.
114953.m: On a bend, tyre friction provides the centripetal force.

114954.q: Use F equals m times v squared divided by r: how big is the centripetal force on a cyclist and her bike of 60 kg at 10 m/s on a bend with a radius of 20 m?
114954.e: F is 60 kg times 10 m/s times 10 m/s divided by 20 m. That gives 6000 divided by 20, so 300 N.
114954.m: You calculate centripetal force as mass times speed squared divided by radius.

114955.q: Why are the bends of a cycling track steeply tilted inwards?
a: So that part of the centripetal force comes from the track
114955.e: On the sloping surface, the track also pushes the riders towards the centre of the bend. So they can ride fast without slipping sideways.
114955.m: Banked bends help provide the centripetal force.

114956.q: What is the inward tilt of a road or track bend towards its inside called?
114956.e: With banking, the outer edge is higher than the inner edge. This allows higher speeds through the bend.
114956.m: Banking raises the outer edge of a bend.

114957.q: Why do runners in the 200 m lean inwards on the bend?
a: So their feet create a force towards the centre of the bend
So they breathe in less air
So they can see the track better
114957.e: Because they lean, their feet push at an angle against the ground. The ground then pushes the runner towards the centre of the bend and keeps him on the track.
114957.m: Leaning into a bend creates the necessary force towards the centre.

114958.q: In which sport is the Fosbury Flop used?
114958.e: The Fosbury Flop is a technique for getting over the bar in the high jump. Today almost all high jumpers jump this way.
114958.m: The Fosbury Flop is a high-jump technique.

114959.q: Who is the Fosbury Flop named after?
114959.e: Dick Fosbury from the USA developed the technique in the 1960s. At first people laughed at him for it.
114959.m: The Fosbury Flop is named after Dick Fosbury.

114960.q: What happened after Dick Fosbury won Olympic gold with his new technique in 1968?
a: The technique spread around the world
114960.e: Fosbury's win convinced coaches and athletes. Within a few years almost all high jumpers were using the Flop.
114960.m: After Fosbury's Olympic win, the Flop spread quickly.

114961.q: How does a jumper cross the bar in the Fosbury Flop?
a: Face down with arms stretched out
114961.e: The jumper turns on take-off and goes over with his back to the bar. Head and shoulders go first, the legs last.
114961.m: In the Fosbury Flop you jump backwards, head first.

114962.q: Why has the Fosbury Flop almost completely replaced older high-jump techniques?
a: You can get higher over the bar with it
You don't need a run-up for it
It is the only technique allowed
114962.e: In the Flop, the body's centre of gravity can even stay below the bar while the body slides over it. So you can clear greater heights with the same strength.
114962.m: You jump higher with the Fosbury Flop.

114963.q: What was needed to make the Fosbury Flop possible without injuries?
a: Soft foam mats to land on
114963.e: In the past, high jumpers landed in sand or sawdust. Only with thick foam mats could you land safely on your back.
114963.m: Without soft mats the Fosbury Flop would be too dangerous.

114964.q: According to the rules, how must a high jumper take off?
a: From standing with a backwards run-up
114964.e: In the high jump only a one-footed take-off is allowed. In the Flop you take off from the foot further from the bar.
114964.m: In the high jump you take off from one foot.

114965.q: Roughly what is the men's high jump world record (as of 2026)?
114965.e: The Cuban Javier Sotomayor cleared 2.45 m in 1993. This record had not been beaten by 2026.
114965.m: The high jump world record is 2.45 m.

114966.q: What does the Magnus effect describe?
a: A spinning ball is pushed sideways
A ball bounces higher on hard ground
A ball gets lighter in water
114966.e: A ball that spins as it flies deflects the air flowing around it. This creates a sideways force, and the flight path curves.
114966.m: Because of the Magnus effect, a spinning ball flies in a curve.

114967.q: What must a flying ball do for the Magnus effect to happen?
a: It must stand still in the air
114967.e: Only a spinning ball deflects the air more on one side than on the other. This creates a sideways force. The effect is named after the physicist Heinrich Gustav Magnus.
114967.m: The Magnus effect only happens with spinning balls.

114968.q: In football, what do you call a ball that curves through the air because of its spin?
114968.e: The player strikes the ball on the side and gives it spin. Because of the Magnus effect, the ball then flies in a curved arc.
114968.m: A banana kick curves through the air because of spin.

114969.q: What does topspin, a forward spin, do to a tennis ball?
114969.e: Forward spin creates a downward force. The ball dips quickly behind the net and can still be hit hard.
114969.m: Topspin makes a tennis ball drop faster.

114970.q: What does backspin do to a golf ball that is hit a long way?
a: It gets lift and flies longer
It falls to the ground at once
114970.e: Through the Magnus effect, backspin creates an upward force. So the ball stays in the air longer.
114970.m: Backspin gives a golf ball lift.

114971.q: Which ship drive uses the Magnus effect with large spinning cylinders instead of sails?
114971.e: With a Flettner rotor, tall cylinders spin in the wind. This creates a sideways force that pulls the ship forwards.
114971.m: The Flettner rotor drives ships using the Magnus effect.

114972.q: How must a footballer strike the ball at a free kick so that it curves?
a: On the side, so it spins
Not at all, he must throw it
114972.e: If you strike the ball on the side, it gets spin. Because of the Magnus effect, it then flies in a curve.
114972.m: A ball struck on the side spins and curves.

114973.q: In the Magnus effect, what creates the force on the ball?
a: Different air flow on the two sides
114973.e: On one side the ball's surface moves with the air, on the other against it. The air is therefore deflected to one side, and the ball feels an opposite force.
114973.m: The Magnus effect comes from uneven air flow around the spinning ball.

114974.q: Why does a spin on the ice still slow down over time?
a: Because of friction from the blade and the air
114974.e: The blade and the air brake the spin a little. As a result, angular momentum is gradually lost.

114975.q: Which conservation law explains the faster spin in a pirouette?
114975.e: Without external torques, a body’s angular momentum stays the same. If the distribution of mass changes, the speed of rotation therefore changes.
114975.m: Angular momentum is conserved in a pirouette.

114976.q: How can a figure skater slow down a spin without putting the other foot down?
114976.e: With arms spread out, the mass is further from the axis of rotation. The moment of inertia gets bigger and the spin slower.
114976.m: Spreading out your arms slows a spin.

114977.q: What is the quantity called that tells you how hard it is to set a body spinning?
114977.e: The moment of inertia depends on the mass and its distance from the axis of rotation. The further out the mass lies, the larger it is.
114977.m: The moment of inertia describes resistance to rotation.

114978.q: A skater halves her moment of inertia by pulling in her arms. How does her speed of rotation change?
114978.e: The product of moment of inertia and speed of rotation stays the same. If one factor is halved, the other must become twice as large.
114978.m: Half the moment of inertia means double the speed of rotation.

114979.q: Which Swiss figure skater gave her name to a spin in which you pull your foot up over your head?
114979.e: Denise Biellmann became world champion in 1981. The Biellmann spin, named after her, is still performed today.
114979.m: The Biellmann spin is named after Denise Biellmann.

114980.q: Why does a diver spin faster in a tucked somersault than in a straight one?
a: Because his moment of inertia is smaller
114980.e: In the tuck, the mass is close to the axis of rotation. As with a skating spin, the smaller moment of inertia leads to faster spinning.
114980.m: You spin faster tucked than stretched out.

114981.q: In figure skating, what is the spin called in which you turn on one leg in a deep crouch?
114981.e: In the sit spin you bend the skating leg deeply and stretch the other leg forwards. The upright spin and the camel spin are the other basic forms.
114981.m: In the sit spin you turn in a deep crouch.

114982.q: At what launch angle does a ball fly furthest without air resistance, if it is thrown and lands at the same height?
